aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-01.text: You settled that in a heartbeat, with no training at all. Philosophy has been working on why for three hundred years.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-03.text: Kant noticed something. Hungry, your hand goes out and takes the apple.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-04.text: The sunset feeds nothing. You want nothing from it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-05.text: You just look. He needed a whole book to say that.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-06.text: Hume admitted beauty lives only in the mind. Then he ranked masters over hacks anyway.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-07.text: Hume’s fix was a panel of trained critics. Watch their verdicts slide together.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-11.text: Now the part where you come in. You rarely stop at saying “I like it”.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-12.text: You say “it is beautiful”, as though it were a fact. One private feeling, eight people summoned to agree.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-00.text: Two hours of the finest film-making you’ve ever sat through. Every frame placed by a master.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-01.text: And all of that skill is working to make cruelty look glorious.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-02.text: Nobody disputes the skill, so the craft verdict is easy to write. Underneath it sits a second question — what all that skill is asking you to feel.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-03.text: Oscar Wilde draws the shutter across that second question. He says a book is well written or badly written, and there’s nothing else on the paper to judge.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-05.text: The moralist shoves the shutter back. What a work invites you to feel isn’t a footnote: it is part of what the work already is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-06.text: A third camp draws a line between the two. Berys Gaut says that if a work asks you to feel what you shouldn’t, it’s flawed as art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-00.text: A gallery hangs two pictures. One was painted by a person over four months.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-01.text: One was generated in about nine seconds.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-02.text: Here they are. Not similar, identical.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-03.text: The same marks in the same places, the same size, the same everything you could photograph.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-04.text: Only the plaques tell the two apart. Cover the plaques and no visitor, curator or critic can sort them reliably.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-06.text: So every visible property is shared. Whatever separates these two isn’t in the object at all, but in how the object came to be here.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-00.text: A poem hangs where anyone can read it. The poet stands across the square and says every reader has got the poem wrong.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-01.text: A reader comes away from the board certain: this is grief. The lamp, the waiting, the going out.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-02.text: Nothing on the page hints at a joke.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-03.text: Every reader who stops adds another mark, and every mark says the same word. Sealed inside the poet’s head is whatever he meant.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-05.text: Now the poet insists the last line was a joke. Two more readers stop, read, and add the same mark.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-06.text: The box still will not open.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-00.text: Two canvases. One is a Vermeer.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-01.text: The other was painted last year by a man called van Meegeren, and no expert in Europe could separate them.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-02.text: Look as long as you like, and there’s no brushstroke to find. The forger was better than the tests, which is why the case is interesting.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-03.text: So draw what you cannot see: where each canvas has been. One line runs back through three and a half centuries of hands.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-04.text: The other starts last year and stops.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-06.text: When van Meegeren confessed in 1947, not a single canvas changed. Paintings called lost masterpieces became cheap fakes overnight.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-00.text: One cask, tasted by a whole room. The verdict comes back unanimous.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-01.text: There’s nothing wrong with this wine.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-02.text: Then two people disagree. One of them tastes iron.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-03.text: The other just finds it too sweet, which isn’t the same kind of complaint at all.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-04.text: Hume begins where most people stop. Taste really does differ, he agrees.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-05.text: Hume refuses to go on and say that every verdict is therefore as good as the next.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-07.text: Cervantes got there first. They drained the cask, and a key was lying at the bottom on a leather thong.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-00.text: A rose, and five things a person might say standing in front of it. Every one of them is honest.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-01.text: Kant isn’t asking which of the five claims is true. He wants to know which one is a judgement of beauty at all.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-02.text: Kant’s test is odd and very simple. Strip away every stake you have in the rose.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-03.text: If the delight is still there, that was beauty.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-04.text: A stake is anything you want from the rose. To own it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-05.text: To sell it. To furnish a room.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-06.text: To be seen standing beside it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-09.text: Cut the other four and the rose doesn’t change. Notice what survived isn’t even “I like it”.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-00.text: You’ve stood in front of this painting three times and liked it more each time. Today you read the label on the wall.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-01.text: There’s the painting. Finished in 1911, and not one mark has moved since.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-02.text: Whatever happens next happens to you, not to the canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-03.text: The first line on the card says the painter took the commission from a man he despised. He said so in a letter.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-05.text: The gallery keeps adding, and now the card is longer than the painting is wide. You notice you’ve been reading it instead of looking.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-00.text: A shape in the dark. Your heart goes, your skin goes cold, and every part of you wants to be somewhere else.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-01.text: On Friday night you pay money for that. The same heart, the same cold skin, and you chose it off a menu.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-02.text: Nothing has been turned down. The meter doesn’t care that this sound arrived inside a frame.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-04.text: Three answers have been offered. The fear is worked through and released.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-05.text: The fear is converted by the telling. The fear is the fee you pay to find out.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-00.text: A piece of music everyone calls sad. Here’s its shape: slow, low, and going down.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-01.text: And here’s a person who has had bad news. Same slope, drawn from the same numbers.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-02.text: That’s the whole theory. You hear the music as sad because it moves the way sadness moves.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-03.text: Now the awkward panel. A shape is not a mood, and there’s nobody inside the notes to be having one.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-06.text: Which leaves a real puzzle. If nothing in there is sad, why do people pay to sit and be made miserable?

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-00.text: Aesthetics has spent most of its life indoors, looking at things in frames. Take the frame outside and point it at whatever happens to be there.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-01.text: A drainpipe. Nobody hung it or signed it, and still the pipe has a shape, a rhythm and a set of stains.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-02.text: Put a frame round the pipe and you’ll look at it properly for the first time.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-03.text: Now a marsh. Flat, buggy, no view.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-04.text: A passerby glances and files it under ugly, and the glance is the whole of their appreciation.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-06.text: So bring the natural history. Nursery, filter, flood defence, one of the densest habitats there is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-07.text: The frame has not moved and the marsh has not moved. The verdict has.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-00.text: A dead painter is making you feel something right now. How does one mind’s feeling cross paint and centuries to reach yours?

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-01.text: Forget beauty and forget skill. Tolstoy calls art an infection.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-02.text: The artist feels something, the work carries it, and you catch it off the work. Collingwood adds that artists often don’t know the feeling until the work is finished.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-03.text: A boy who met a wolf tells the story so well the room is frightened too. For Tolstoy that’s art, but only if the boy means every word.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-06.text: If they’re right, a feeling can be packed into lines and sounds and words. It then outlives the person, the language and the century.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-07.text: Almost nothing else anybody builds does that.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-00.text: Four reasons people give for why art is worth the money. Watch each one get answered by something cheaper.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-01.text: Art teaches you things. So does a textbook, faster and with fewer mistakes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-02.text: Art records how the world looked. A camera does the same.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-03.text: Art decorates a room, and wallpaper is cheaper.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-04.text: Three struck out, and nothing came for the fourth.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-07.text: One warning about the method. Something can be replaceable and still be worth having.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-00.text: Three works: six printings, four recordings, one canvas. In a moment all of it burns.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-01.text: Now start burning. Every copy of the novel, every recording of the symphony, and the painting on the wall.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-02.text: Two of the three works survived. You could print the novel again tomorrow from the text.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-03.text: The painting cannot come back. There was never a text to print it from.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-07.text: Then photography walks in and makes a mess of it. Many prints come from one negative, and people still queue for the first one.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-00.text: The lights go down. Green slime starts oozing towards the camera, and it’s coming for you.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-01.text: Take the readings. The heart rate goes up.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-02.text: The belief that any of the story is real never leaves the floor.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-03.text: Three claims all seem true. You feel real fear.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-04.text: Feeling needs belief. You believe none of the film.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-06.text: One answer says you were never afraid. You were playing a game, and inside the game your fear is fictional.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-08.text: The rival answer keeps the feeling and drops the middle claim. Vividly imagining a thing is enough to move you.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-00.text: Seven notes, no words. It can move you to tears.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-01.text: Now try to say what it was about.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-02.text: A mood, easily. Slow drooping lines sound sorrowful, the way a slow drooping person does.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-03.text: A bird, sometimes. Trilling violins can imitate birdsong, though the printed title is doing most of the pointing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-05.text: Most instrumental music works this way. The music is not about anything.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-06.text: The music is a shape made of tones.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-08.text: That’s the grand objection. Music points at nothing you can see because it copies the wanting underneath everything.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-00.text: One panel, in one room, where it has hung for five hundred years. People cross oceans to stand in front of it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-01.text: A print, a poster, a screen, a feed. The same picture everywhere at once, and none of them is here.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-02.text: What the copies leave behind has a name. Walter Benjamin called it the aura, and it is not about quality.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-04.text: An altarpiece sat in one church and pilgrims travelled to it. A film has no original print to travel to.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-06.text: Benjamin wasn’t only mourning. Cut loose from one room, a work reaches everybody, and it can argue rather than decorate.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-00.text: Name the thing you find most beautiful. A sociologist will guess where you grew up.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-01.text: Two visitors stand at the same canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-02.text: One reads it at once. The other doesn’t know where to start.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-03.text: Pierre Bourdieu asked what each of them walked in carrying.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-05.text: Bourdieu called it cultural capital. Books at home, gallery trips, the talk at the table.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-06.text: Cultural capital arrives so early it feels like your own eye.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-08.text: Kant praised a pure pleasure in form. Bourdieu answered that only some people can afford one.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-00.text: A plastic flamingo on a lawn. Nobody’s calling it great sculpture.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-01.text: Kitsch hands you the feeling already chewed. A kitten with enormous wet eyes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-02.text: Milan Kundera called it the second tear. The first is for children on the grass, the second for how nice it feels to be moved.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-03.text: Camp is the other thing entirely. Kitsch is sincere, and camp is a wink.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-05.text: Susan Sontag mapped camp: drag, B-movies, a chandelier hung in a diner.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-07.text: The same flamingo can be either. One neighbour finds it lovely, and another finds it gloriously absurd.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-00.text: First a melody, then a noise. Then four minutes of a pianist playing nothing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-01.text: Avant-garde is a military word. It named the guard sent first into open country.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-02.text: Cubism broke perspective. Atonal music dropped the key, and poetry dropped the sentence.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-03.text: The gamble is that habit dulls a person. You stop seeing what you have seen a thousand times.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-05.text: John Cage sat at a piano in 1952 and played nothing for four minutes and thirty-three seconds.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-07.text: Impressionism was mocked as unfinished smears. It now sells more postcards than anything.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-00.text: You haven’t been to a museum in months. You’ve had aesthetic experiences all week.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-01.text: The smell of rain. A tidy desk, and the arc of a pass nobody expected.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-02.text: For centuries aesthetics meant paintings, symphonies and poems. Most of a life happens elsewhere.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-03.text: Cooking, dressing, tidying, commuting. Yuriko Saito argues these hours deserve the same attention.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-05.text: A footballer threads a pass nobody expected, and the stadium gasps. Grace, timing, form that fits its purpose.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-07.text: A critic objects. If a tidy drawer and a Rembrandt are both aesthetic, the word has stopped working.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-00.text: It never happened. A war that was never fought, soldiers who never lived, and you learned something.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-01.text: Fiction is false on its face. So the puzzle is how anything true gets out of it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-02.text: Plato wanted the poets exiled. He argued that art copies a copy and stirs feeling over reason.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-03.text: A textbook tells you that grief exists. A novel puts you inside it for four hundred pages.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-05.text: A reader finishes a war novel and says she understands those soldiers now.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-07.text: A sceptic answers that she learned nothing. The soldiers are invented, so the lesson was her own feeling.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-00.text: No culture has ever lived without song or story. Not one, anywhere.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-01.text: That’s strange enough to want an explanation.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-02.text: Tragedy hurts, and you go anyway. Aristotle says it raises pity and fear in you, then works them back out of you.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-03.text: Aristotle named the effect katharsis. He never quite says what katharsis is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-04.text: Athens watches Oedipus work out that he killed his own father. Nobody looks away.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-05.text: Aristotle thinks you can bear to look at painful things drawn well because looking at them teaches you something.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-07.text: A minor key floods you with sadness and never argues for it. Schopenhauer thought music reaches something underneath all the arguing — the restless wanting that drives you.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-08.text: For Plato, that same thing made music dangerous.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-00.text: You could live without beauty. Food keeps you alive and shelter keeps you safe.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-01.text: So what does beauty keep? One answer calls it decoration, and the first thing cut when life gets hard.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-02.text: Iris Murdoch answered differently. A kestrel hovering pulls a person straight out of their own head.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-03.text: Murdoch called it unselfing. The anxious ego steps back and something real outside it takes the room.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-05.text: Travellers in Florence have reported dizziness and racing hearts. Beauty can land like an event.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-07.text: Learning to attend properly to a bird is practice for attending properly to a person.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-00.text: Nine notes on four strings. A good phrase, played well, and the room is pleased with it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-01.text: The applause is polite. Nobody stands up.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-02.text: Now three of the strings are gone. Same nine notes, same tempo, same phrasing — every sound leaving the instrument is the sound that left it before.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-04.text: And the room is on its feet. Not one sound reaching anybody’s ears had changed.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-05.text: The meter is the only thing on stage that moved.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-00.text: Nine years of a life, one bar each. This one starts badly and saves its best years for last.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-01.text: Here’s the same life run backwards. The same nine years, in the opposite order.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-02.text: Nothing has been added and nothing taken away.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-03.text: And a third, level throughout — never bad, never remarkable. Nine identical years that come to the same amount as the other two.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-05.text: The line sits at the same height in all three, because all three hold the same amount of good. A ledger cannot tell them apart.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-00.text: A painting four hundred years old, hanging as the centuries left it. Dark, and a little hard to read.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-01.text: What’s on it is a stack. Paint at the bottom, then the painter’s glaze, then varnish, then centuries of smoke and dust.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-02.text: Take the dirt off and nobody objects. It isn’t part of the work, and everyone agrees the painter didn’t put it there.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-03.text: Keep going and the argument starts. When the Sistine ceiling was cleaned, startling pinks came out.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-04.text: Some scholars said a deliberate final glaze had just been scrubbed off for ever.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-07.text: It doesn’t help to say “just return it to the original”. No layer arrives labelled as the one the painter stopped at.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-00.text: A bull, drawn properly. Eleven strokes, and nobody has to be told what it is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-01.text: First, what makes it a picture of a bull? Not resemblance, because two twins resemble each other and neither is a picture of the other.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-02.text: Now take strokes away. Picasso did this in 1945, eleven plates of the same animal, each one with less in it than the last.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-03.text: And the final plate is a handful of lines that is still unmistakably a bull. Nobody can say which plate would have been the first one that was not.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-06.text: So convention and context do most of the work. You’ve been taught how a bull is drawn, and three lines are enough to hand you the rest.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-00.text: A joke is a piece of track. The setup runs you along it, and you already know where you’re going.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-01.text: Here’s the setup line. “I told my doctor I broke my arm in two places.”

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-02.text: You’re in a surgery now, waiting for the diagnosis.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-04.text: Both readings had to fit. That’s the part people miss.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-05.text: A punchline that doesn’t fit the setup is not surprising. It’s wrong.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-07.text: Now watch it with the second line drawn in first. Same words, same swap, and nothing happens.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-08.text: That is what explaining a joke does to it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-09.text: That’s why the old theories only half work. Hobbes said we laugh at someone beneath us.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-10.text: Freud said we let out pressure.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-00.text: One square, one afternoon. Packed at one end of the day, empty at the other.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-01.text: Everything you can see is real.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-03.text: Nothing was altered. No pixel was moved.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-04.text: Both prints are accurate and they disagree about what happened.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-05.text: Photographs get this power from feeling transparent. Light came off the thing and landed here.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-06.text: So you say you are seeing the square, not a record of it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-09.text: A painting nobody suspects of neutrality does less damage here. You know a painter chose.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-10.text: You forget that a photographer did.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-00.text: Two performances tonight. The top one was written first, and every note existed before anybody walked on.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-01.text: The bottom row is a solo. Watch the line arrive with nothing above it and nothing to compare it against.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-03.text: That’s why you can burn every copy of a symphony and it survives. Do that to an improvisation and there’s nothing left to recover.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-05.text: Then recording arrived, and players started learning famous solos note for note. Something meant to happen once now had a correct version.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-07.text: So the same sounds become a different kind of thing depending on what stood behind them. Not how the sounds strike the ear.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-00.text: You’ve seen this one. You know he gets out of the building.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-01.text: Two bars a scene. What you know runs flat and full from the opening frame, and what you feel climbs anyway.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-02.text: Three claims, and they cannot all stand.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-04.text: Greek crowds knew the myths by heart. Nobody in the seats sat wondering how it would end.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-05.text: Coleridge had a phrase for what an audience does instead, and it is not forgetting.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-00.text: A chair and a sculpture can be the same wood, the same hands and the same skill.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-01.text: So look at the making instead. Each of these is a plan at the top and the hours it took underneath.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-02.text: And here’s what came out of each one.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-04.text: That’s Collingwood’s line between art and craft. It’s drawn in the making, never in the thing that comes out.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-05.text: Immanuel Kant had drawn it a century and a half earlier, and put the difference in one word: freedom.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-00.text: In 1917, a plain urinal was entered as art. No carving, no painting, just a choice.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-02.text: For ages there were two answers. Plato said art copies the world skilfully, and the Greek word for that is mimesis.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-03.text: Tolstoy said art puts a feeling into a form somebody else can pick up. Both assume a person made it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-04.text: Duchamp laid a urinal on its back, signed it R. Mutt 1917, and sent the thing in.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-05.text: The committee hid the piece. An unsigned defence replied that the maker didn’t matter.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-06.text: Duchamp chose the object, and choosing was the work.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-08.text: Fountain fits neither answer. It copies nothing and expresses nothing, and it still will not go away.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-09.text: Asking “but is that art?” is already philosophy. It makes you say what you secretly think art is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-00.text: Nobody hangs a dinner in a gallery. There’s an old reason for that.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-01.text: Hegel split the senses in two. Sight and hearing went on one side.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-02.text: Smell, taste and touch went on the other, and stayed there for two centuries.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-03.text: Looking leaves a painting standing. Eating does not leave the dinner standing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-05.text: A tasting menu opens somewhere, develops, quotes an older dish and closes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-07.text: Diners argue about whether the fifth course earned its place. That’s following a form.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-00.text: Point at the edge of a painting, then say whether your finger is on it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-01.text: The canvas is the work and the wall is the room. The frame is the trouble.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-02.text: Kant had a word for it. A parergon is a thing beside the work, like drapery on a statue.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-03.text: A frame is not a part. The painting would be the same painting without one.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-05.text: The frame is not outside either. A gilt frame and a steel one make the same canvas read differently.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-07.text: And the border keeps widening. The title, the wall card, the height, the museum itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-00.text: You look at the world all day, yet rarely see it. Aesthetics trains your attention until the eye wakes up.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-01.text: Murdoch took the idea from Simone Weil. Attention is a just and loving look at one real thing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-02.text: The obstacle is what Murdoch calls the fat, relentless ego. Attention is what quiets it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-03.text: A woman is at a window, brooding over a bruise to her pride, when she sees a hovering kestrel. In a moment the brooding is gone.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-04.text: Nothing left but kestrel. She called that unselfing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-07.text: Ruskin wrote that drawing recovers “the innocence of the eye”. You see patches of colour as they are, before the mind swaps in its idea.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-08.text: Ruskin’s students studied one leaf before any tree.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-00.text: A storm at sea is terrifying, so why do you stop to watch it? Some experiences thrill you because they dwarf you.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-01.text: Burke split your reactions in two. A flower is beautiful: small, smooth, pleasing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-02.text: A storm or a vast mountain is sublime. It overwhelms, mixing terror with a strange delight.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-03.text: Stand on a cliff in a gale. The drop could kill you, yet you’re safe.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-04.text: Real danger held at a distance is a pleasure of its own, and nothing gentle feels like it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-07.text: Kant moved the awe inward. The mountain does overwhelm your senses.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-08.text: But Kant says the real jolt is your mind finding room for something so vast. The mountain is not the sublime thing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-00.text: Someone glances at the scribble, then at the masterwork, and says the scribble is better. You want to say that’s wrong.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-02.text: Three seconds made one of these. Thirty years made the other.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-03.text: Nearly everyone who walks in here feels the gap. But a feeling is not yet a reason.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-04.text: Hume went looking for the beauty in the paint and came back empty. Scrape the canvas, weigh it, measure it: no beauty comes off.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-05.text: It happens in the mind doing the looking.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-07.text: If beauty only happens in minds, your friend’s mind is as full of it as anyone’s. So the scribble ties with the masterwork.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-08.text: Something in you refuses the tie. Hume refused it too.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-10.text: So Hume set a bar. A verdict counts when it comes from long practice, wide comparison, no personal grudges, and plain good sense.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-11.text: Where people like that agree, you have a standard.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-12.text: This is not snobbery. A wine taster does taste notes you can’t, because practice reshapes perception itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-13.text: Stand here again after a hundred galleries and this canvas will show you more than it does today.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-00.text: Two people stare at the same painting. One says it works because of the shapes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-01.text: The other says the painting works because it aches. Same canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-02.text: Two reasons with nothing in common.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-03.text: Luckily there’s a pair of glasses on the wall for each of them. Take the first pair down.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-04.text: Nothing mystical. They just change what you notice.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-05.text: Through these, the painting is pure arrangement. A block here, an edge there, one shape leaning on another.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-06.text: Whatever the picture shows has gone silent.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-07.text: Hang that pair up. There’s a second pair on the same wall.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-08.text: It’s about to show you a different painting, on the same canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-09.text: Now the blocks dissolve into strokes. You’re not measuring anything.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-10.text: You’re catching a mood, as if the painter handed you what they were feeling that afternoon.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-12.text: That way of looking has a name: formalism. Clive Bell claimed every real work of visual art shares one thing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-13.text: Bell called it significant form: an arrangement of line and colour that moves you. The subject is beside the point.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-15.text: The second pair has a name too. Tolstoy said art is one person handing a feeling to another.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-16.text: Collingwood added a twist. The painter often finds the feeling only by painting the picture.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-00.text: For most of the history of art, one word did the deciding. Beautiful things were art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-02.text: Then in 1964 Andy Warhol stacked plywood boxes painted to look exactly like Brillo cartons. Not a copy of a beautiful thing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-04.text: Arthur Danto stood in front of the two boxes and asked the question that broke the old rule. The boxes are identical.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-05.text: One is in a supermarket and one is in a gallery. You can’t tell which is the art by looking.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-07.text: So the difference is not in the object. It’s in what the object does: the argument the work makes, the moment it lands in, the history it answers.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-08.text: Beauty came off the throne and became one option among many.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-00.text: You say you know it. But what is knowing?

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-01.text: That question is the whole of epistemology. Plato was already pressing it in the Theaetetus.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-02.text: The standard recipe has three locks. The claim is true.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-03.text: You believe it. And you have justification — solid reasons.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-04.text: Turn all three and the door opens: you know.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-05.text: Strip the reasons and it collapses. A true belief held for no reason is luck wearing a disguise.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-06.text: Justification ties your belief to the truth on purpose.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-07.text: Socrates makes the case with a jury. The jurors are talked into a verdict that happens to be true, and never saw a thing.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-08.text: Two locks turn. The door holds.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-00.text: You’re not certain the sun will rise tomorrow. You’d still bet everything you own on it.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-01.text: So do you know, or don’t you?

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-02.text: One old answer draws the line at absolute certainty, where you couldn’t possibly be wrong. Held strictly, that leaves almost nothing: not the sunrise, not your own name.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-03.text: Fallibilism moves the line. You can know something and still admit you might be wrong.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-04.text: Knowing and doubting are allowed in the room together.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-06.text: Watch what science does with doubt. Science never claims certainty, and it plainly knows a great deal.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-07.text: Evidence arrives and the needle moves. Changing its mind is how the method works, not a sign of failure.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-00.text: You glance up at the hallway clock. Three o’clock, and it really is three o’clock.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-01.text: You have never been more right, or for a worse reason.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-02.text: You step across for a second look. The other dial has moved on, but the hallway clock hasn’t.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-03.text: It stopped twelve hours ago, at three.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-04.text: Still, count what you had. You believed it.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-05.text: It was true. And a clock on a wall is an ordinary reason to trust one.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-08.text: Walk on, and watch the pair. They agreed for one instant and never will again.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-09.text: Nothing ever joined your reason to the fact. The match was an accident.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-00.text: You’ve never seen an atom, and you weren’t there for your own birth. You’d still bet money on both.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-01.text: So how did they get in?

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-02.text: Rain lands on your hand and you believe it’s raining before you’ve thought about it. That pipe is short: the world touches you, and the belief is already in.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-03.text: You know what you ate this morning, but the toast is long gone. What you are reading is a copy your mind kept.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-04.text: That pipe is longer, and it bends.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-06.text: The third pipe doesn’t begin near you at all. It runs in from strangers — teachers, books, mapmakers, people long dead.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-07.text: Now watch what it does to the level.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-00.text: A fair lottery, a million tickets, one winner. You hold ticket forty thousand and one.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-01.text: Will it win? You’d say no, flatly, and you’d be right.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-02.text: Here are twenty of them, to keep the drawing manageable. Nothing about the argument changes with the count.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-03.text: Strike the first one out, at a million to one. It’s still not certainty, but it beats most things you happily claim to know, like who your neighbours are.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-05.text: The same reasoning covers every ticket, so strike them all. Read the grid now.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-06.text: You’ve just said this draw has no winner, and you know there’s one.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-00.text: Here’s your situation, drawn honestly. There’s the world, and there’s what reaches you of the world, with a leap in between.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-01.text: Everything you’ve ever checked, you checked by looking. So every check happened here, on this side of the glass, and never against the world itself.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-02.text: So the world is not something you observe. It’s something you infer, across this gap, from what shows up on the screen.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-04.text: Now swap the world for a tank and a very good computer. Watch the screen while it happens.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-05.text: Nothing on the screen moved, and nothing on it ever would.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-00.text: Two questions about anything you know. Did you need to look?

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-01.text: And does it tell you something, or only unpack a word?

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-02.text: Three of the boxes fill straight away. Bachelors are unmarried.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-03.text: The chair is over there. And the fourth box is supposed to be empty.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-04.text: Empty because of an old rule. If you did not have to look, you learned nothing new.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-05.text: If you learned something new, you had to look.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-07.text: Kant drops one card into the empty box. Seven plus five is twelve.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-08.text: You ran no experiment, and twelve was not sitting inside seven and five.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-00.text: Here’s every answer the 1919 eclipse could have come back with. Starlight bends by this much, or that much, or not at all.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-01.text: Now three theories, each drawn as wide as the answers it allows. Two of them have bet almost the whole row on being right.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-02.text: The third allows everything. Whatever came back, it would have fitted.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-03.text: That’s usually said as a boast.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-05.text: The eclipse came back at one and three-quarter seconds of arc. One narrow bar survived and one narrow bar died.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-00.text: A theory draws a frame around the facts it explains. Inside the frame, everything behaves.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-01.text: Then the awkward results pile up outside the frame. Nobody throws the frame away.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-02.text: Scientists patch the frame, add a circle, and patch it again.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-03.text: Kuhn looked at what actually happened in history. Most of science is not testing the frame.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-04.text: Science is working comfortably inside a frame. Kuhn called the frame a paradigm.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-06.text: Then the whole thing goes at once. Copernicus moved the sun to the middle, and every fact on the board reorganised without one of them moving.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-00.text: Two claims, and you believe one of them far more than the other. That’s the top rail and the bottom one.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-01.text: Look at what’s holding each marker. The round earth is tied to almost everything else you know.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-02.text: The keys are tied to a memory of putting them down.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-03.text: Now the same piece of evidence arrives at both. Somebody you trust tells you it isn’t so.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-04.text: The same report should not move both markers the same distance. The evidence alone can’t decide how far.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-06.text: This is the rule Bayes wrote down. A new fact moves you in proportion to how loosely you were holding on.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-00.text: Five people, and every one of them knows something you don’t.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-01.text: A question turns up, cut to fit only one of these doors. Standing at the wrong door will open nothing.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-02.text: Here’s the everyday failure. A famous heart doctor is asked about diet on television, and answers.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-03.text: Nobody lied. The credentials are real.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-07.text: Then the hard case. Two people behind the right door, both qualified, saying opposite things.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-00.text: You have read every word ever written about swimming. The physics, the technique, the breathing.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-02.text: Start with one instruction, and make it a good one. Precise, true, and easy to check.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-03.text: Below it, the thing the instruction is for.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-04.text: Add the rest. Every line is accurate and you’ve memorised all of them.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-05.text: Look at the box underneath: nothing has arrived in it.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-07.text: Then the reading stops and the hands move, and the box fills. Ryle’s point: not one line of that column is what filled it.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-00.text: You read something surprising. One source, and you hold it loosely.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-01.text: Then three more say it. A paper, a friend, a podcast.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-02.text: The bar climbs, and it’s right to climb.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-03.text: Now the wiring. Three of those four are repeating the same original post.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-04.text: Nobody retracted anything. All four still say the same thing.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-05.text: The real count was never four.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-08.text: A feed is built to show you what people like you already share. It manufactures this picture by default.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-00.text: Right now, believe that rain is falling outside. Not picture rain, not say the words.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-01.text: Take a moment and try your hardest.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-02.text: Here’s the needle. It sits where your belief is, and at the moment it’s parked hard against doubt.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-04.text: Load the first tray with everything you’ve got. Wanting rain.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-05.text: Deciding on rain. Saying the words again.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-06.text: A fortune riding on the answer. The tray fills and the needle does not move.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-08.text: Now one thing in the other tray: rain on the window. You did nothing, wanted nothing, decided nothing, yet the needle goes all the way across.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-00.text: Two people want the same address. One asks somebody who knows it.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-02.text: Both arrive. Both now believe something true, and today there’s nothing to choose between them.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-03.text: Look underneath. One route is a road.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-04.text: The other is a line of stepping stones with nothing between them.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-06.text: Plato asked the same about statues that run away unless you tie them down. A tethered opinion stays put.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-08.text: So the extra value is not in today at all. It’s in every other day, and you can draw it.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-00.text: Claims arrive all day. What you end up believing is whatever is left in the tray.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-01.text: Open the mouth and more gets a hearing. Nothing about that decides how much you keep.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-02.text: Tighten the mesh and most of it goes through the sides. The mouth has not moved.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-04.text: Close the mouth and the mesh has nothing to do. That’s a person who’s never wrong and never learns anything.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-06.text: So the virtue is a pair of settings held at once, and neither one on its own is worth having.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-00.text: A sceptical argument, set out properly. Three premises and a conclusion, and the step from one to the next is fine.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-01.text: Beside each claim, a bar for how sure you are. Not how clever it sounds.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-03.text: Moore holds up his hand and says he knows this. That claim has a longer bar than anything on the ladder.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-06.text: An argument runs both ways. Doubt the conclusion harder than the premises, and it’s the premises that have to move.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-07.text: The sceptic can answer that. He says the bar beside the hand is confidence, not knowledge, and that difference is what’s in dispute.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-00.text: You’ve got a test for what counts as knowledge. So how did you check the test?

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-01.text: Say the ruler is proof. Then the proof needs a ruler of its own.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-02.text: And that one needs another. The line goes down as far as you care to look.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-03.text: Sextus Empiricus reached the bottom and found nothing standing there.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-05.text: The methodist picks the rule first, then lets it sort every belief below.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-06.text: The particularist runs it the other way: cases first, then a rule built to fit them.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-08.text: Neither door is proved. Each one simply begins, and admits it.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-00.text: You and a friend split a dinner bill in your heads. You get forty-three.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-01.text: Your friend gets forty-five. You’re both careful, and both good at sums.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-02.text: That makes her an epistemic peer. Same evidence, same competence, same care.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-03.text: So you can’t assume she blundered. By definition she’s as likely to be right.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-05.text: The disagreement is itself a piece of evidence. A mind as good as yours read the same bill.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-07.text: Steadfasters answer that a well-weighed view may stand. Otherwise any contrarian wins.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-00.text: You can wrong somebody without telling a single lie. Refusing to believe a speaker is enough.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-01.text: A patient describes her symptoms accurately. The report is true and well put.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-02.text: The doctor hears anxiety, because the patient is young. Her word is worth less on arrival.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-03.text: Miranda Fricker gave the wrong a name: testimonial injustice. A bias marks down what a speaker says.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-05.text: There’s a second kind, and it lands earlier. Sometimes a group has no words for what happened.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-07.text: Before anybody said the words “sexual harassment”, victims could feel the wrong and not name it.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-00.text: Your mind is not always a scientist. Sometimes it is a lawyer with the verdict already chosen.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-01.text: A study says your favourite habit is harmful. You check the sample size, the method, the funding.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-02.text: A second study says the habit is fine. You nod and share it without a single question.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-03.text: Same quality of evidence, two different standards. What decided was not the data but the wanting.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-05.text: Motivated reasoning almost never announces itself. You don’t feel biased, you feel right.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-07.text: The verdict came first, and the reasons were recruited afterwards. The search was rigged before it began.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-00.text: You can memorise every fact on the page and understand none of it.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-01.text: Two cooks know the recipe word for word. One panics when the sauce splits.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-02.text: The other rescues it in seconds. Same facts in both heads, and only one of them grasps the dish.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-03.text: Understanding is knowing why. Seeing how the pieces hold each other up is what lets it travel.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-05.text: A student aces the physics test by memorising answers. A new problem defeats her completely.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-07.text: Every fact she has is correct, and the facts sit there in a heap. Nothing carries them to a new case.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-00.text: What if everything you’re sure of is a lie? Descartes doubted it all on purpose, then rebuilt knowledge from the rubble.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-01.text: First he separates two things you run together. Feeling certain is something happening in you.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-02.text: Truth is how the world is. Those two can come apart, so he goes hunting for beliefs that survive every possible doubt.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-03.text: So he imagines a demon of utmost power rigging his whole reality. Every sight, every memory, even that two plus three make five — all could be a planted lie.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-06.text: The demon is a tool, not a real fear. Of each idea Descartes asks: could the demon fake this?

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-08.text: Used this way, doubt rebuilds rather than ruins.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-00.text: Thirty lessons in, the question changed on you.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-01.text: You stopped asking what knowledge is. You started asking how to know well.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-02.text: A wise knower is not the one holding the most facts. Good intellectual character is the skill.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-03.text: Humble about being wrong, curious enough to keep looking, fair enough to credit other people.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-05.text: The oracle called Socrates the wisest man in Athens, and he spent years trying to prove it wrong.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-07.text: Hold a belief firmly enough to act on it, and loosely enough to give it up.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-00.text: You’re already down the road when it hits you: did you lock the door? You can picture doing it.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-01.text: That picture is the only evidence you have.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-02.text: So you check. You open the memory and there it is — the key, the turn, the pull on the handle.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-04.text: But how do you know the memory is any good? You remember checking it.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-05.text: That’s a second drawer, in the same cabinet, made of the same stuff as the first.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-07.text: And a third. Every certificate memory can issue is signed by memory.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-08.text: Meanwhile the door itself has been standing over there the whole time.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-00.text: Four maps of the same stretch of coast. One coastline, drawn four times at four scales.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-01.text: The first is the whole country in one stroke. Nothing on it is false.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-03.text: The second gives you the shape and its bays. The third gives you every rock.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-04.text: It’s also the sort of map you’d still be reading when the tide came in.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-06.text: And here’s the perfect one. One to one, nothing omitted, no error anywhere in it.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-07.text: At that scale the frame holds a single rock.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-00.text: A friend asks whether the bank opens on Saturday. You were there last Saturday and there was a queue out of the door.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-01.text: That’s your evidence, and it’s ordinary. You say you know, nobody blinks, and the two of you carry on.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-02.text: Now the same afternoon with one thing added. A cheque has to clear by Monday or you lose the house.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-03.text: Look at the column as you get out of the car to check. Not one brick has moved.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-04.text: You’ve got the same evidence you had a minute ago.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-07.text: So there is no single height that counts as knowing. There’s a height for this conversation, and it goes up when the answer starts to cost something.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-00.text: Two bars. The left one is what you say.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-01.text: The right one is how often what you say turns out to hold.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-02.text: Down here the two bars agree. Call a thing a coin flip and it lands heads about half the time.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-04.text: Now say you’re certain. The left bar goes to the top.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-05.text: The right one doesn’t follow, and the space between them is the whole subject.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-06.text: Being well calibrated means those two bars match. Notice that’s not the same as being right often.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-07.text: Someone who’s right half the time and says so has both bars level.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-10.text: Here’s the useful part. A match can be fixed from either end, and the end you control today is the left one.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-00.text: A zoo, a pen, a striped animal. You know what that is, and you knew it before you finished looking.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-02.text: Here’s the rule that makes the puzzle awkward. Know a thing.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-03.text: Know what the thing rules out. You should know the second thing as well.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-07.text: Notice what didn’t happen. You never checked for paint.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-08.text: You’d think it strange to be asked, and you’d still say you knew.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-09.text: One way out says the mule was never a live option. If it’s far-fetched enough, your ordinary looking already counts as ruling it out.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-00.text: A counter with four pairs of stockings laid out. All four pairs are identical.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-03.text: Now the interesting part. Every shopper had a reason ready.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-06.text: The cause was position in the row. Told as much, the shoppers said no.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-07.text: Not defensively, not caught out. The reason was invisible from the inside.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-09.text: The shoppers were not lying and were not confused. Each one knew which pair she preferred.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-10.text: The reason for the preference was the part nobody could see.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-11.text: So the gap fills itself, with the only material lying about: the stockings. A reason is built, and it arrives feeling like a memory.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-00.text: An old ship, due to carry emigrants. Her owner has five separate reasons to doubt she’s sound.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-02.text: Watch what he did. He did not inspect her.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-03.text: The owner put the doubts down, one at a time, until they stopped bothering him.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-04.text: Then he took his fee, waved her off, and grieved sincerely when she went down. He never lied to anybody, including himself.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-06.text: Now run it again and let her arrive. Same hull, same cracks, same owner.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-07.text: Look at the verdict card. It has not moved.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-09.text: Both are right about different cases. What survives is the shipowner: when other people carry the risk, the checking is not optional.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-00.text: Three people were asked the time. All three answered, and two of them were right.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-01.text: The solid mark is what each of them believed. The hollow ones are what the same method would have given a minute either side.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-02.text: So one face holds a hit and another holds an aim. Nothing on the stage tells a hit from an aim.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-04.text: A belief is safe when it would still have been true in the cases nearest to this one.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-05.text: The hall clock stopped at ten past four, and you look at it at ten past four. Careful method, true belief, and wrong at almost any other moment.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-00.text: Three judges hear one case. A verdict of liable needs two findings: a contract existed, and it was broken.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-01.text: Each of them votes on both, and each verdict follows from the two votes above it. Nobody is careless.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-04.text: The puzzle has a name: the doctrinal paradox. Each row can hold together while the row you get by counting does not.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-05.text: So a court has to choose what it counts. It can count the verdict alone, or count the reasons and let the verdict follow.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-00.text: Blank mind at birth, or already primed? Two camps, the empiricists and the rationalists, have never once stopped arguing about it.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-01.text: Locke pictured the newborn mind as a sheet of blank paper. Everything that arrives on it later gets there by being seen, felt or thought over.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-03.text: You learn the word hot by getting burned, and red by seeing red. Big ideas grow from small sensations, written onto a page that started blank.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-05.text: The other camp fires back. Some things you never had to be shown.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-06.text: Descartes and Leibniz thought maths and logic get worked out by reason alone, before experience gets a say. That is what a priori means.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-07.text: Plato has Socrates walk an untaught boy through doubling a square, using nothing but questions. Nobody teaches him any geometry.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-08.text: So Plato says learning is remembering what was in there already.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-10.text: Then Kant brokered a truce, and said both were half right. The raw material does pour in through the senses.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-11.text: But the mind pours that raw material into forms of its own: space, time and cause. Neither sense nor mind works alone.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-00.text: You test an idea and the test comes back wrong. Something in there is false.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-01.text: But an idea never reaches the evidence on its own.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-02.text: It brings the lens, the sums, and a hundred unspoken assumptions about the setup.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-03.text: So the failed prediction convicts all of them at once. Pierre Duhem saw it first.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-05.text: Uranus once moved wrongly. Le Verrier kept Newton and blamed a planet nobody had seen.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-07.text: Neptune turned up where he pointed. Then Mercury wobbled, and the same move found nothing.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-00.text: Hold a straight oar up. Nothing to report.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-01.text: Put half the oar in water and the shaft kinks at the surface.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-02.text: The argument is three steps. What you see is bent, and the oar is not.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-03.text: So what you see is not the oar. Something else is standing in front of it.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-05.text: Bertrand Russell accepted the conclusion and named the thing you see a sense-datum.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-07.text: J. L. Austin answered that looking bent is one of the ways a straight oar looks.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-00.text: Aristotle opens his largest book with the line “All men by nature desire to know”. It’s a claim about you.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-01.text: Nobody taught you to want to know things.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-02.text: The best kind of knowing, he says, isn’t the useful kind. It’s the kind you want for no reason beyond wanting it.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-03.text: Aristotle calls knowing for its own sake the only free knowledge. It’s in service of nothing.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-04.text: Aristotle’s evidence is small and hard to argue with. You like looking at things.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-05.text: Not to get anything out of it. You just do, and that plain pleasure is where the whole ladder starts.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-06.text: Both Plato and Aristotle say philosophy begins in wonder. Not the pleasant kind.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-07.text: Their word is closer to being knocked off balance by something you can’t account for.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-08.text: Centuries later Francis Bacon points the whole ladder somewhere else. Knowledge is for getting things done, and for making nature do what you want.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-09.text: Aristotle wanted to understand nature. Bacon wanted to use it.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-00.text: What if every belief can be doubted? The ancient skeptics took that idea further than Descartes ever did.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-01.text: Skepticism asks whether you can know anything at all. For every reason to believe, the skeptic finds an equal reason to doubt.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-02.text: If the reasons cancel out, how can any belief be secure?

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-03.text: Pyrrho met each claim with its opposite, found both equally strong, and refused to decide. He called the refusal epoche.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-04.text: What he got out of it wasn’t despair but calm — ataraxia.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-07.text: But total doubt eats itself. If nothing can be known, how could you know even that?

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-08.text: So most sceptics doubt softly. They go after your confidence, not after the chance of ever knowing anything.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-00.text: The sun rose today. Will it rise tomorrow?

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-01.text: You feel sure. But Hume asks what gives you the right to be.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-02.text: Induction goes from the cases you’ve seen to the ones you haven’t. Every swan so far was white, so all swans are white.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-03.text: Science runs on that leap constantly.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-04.text: Why expect the future to match the past? Only because it always has.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-05.text: But that uses the past to vouch for the past. The circle closes, and logic never gets a grip on it.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-07.text: A chicken is fed every morning and grows sure the farmer is its friend. Each feeding confirms the rule — until the day the farmer wrings its neck.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-08.text: More of the same is no guarantee of the same.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-00.text: Your friend swears the bus comes at eight. You ask why.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-01.text: Your friend answers. You ask why again.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-02.text: How many times can he do that before he runs out?

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-03.text: Every answer he gives is just another belief. And a belief holds nothing up unless something holds it up first.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-04.text: So off he goes to fetch one.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-05.text: Your friend wedges it underneath: the timetable says so. Support goes under, never on top, so this tower grows downward.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-06.text: And now the timetable is a belief that needs propping up too.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-07.text: Back to the pile. Why trust the timetable?

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-08.text: The city printed it. Why trust the city?

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-09.text: You can already hear the next why coming.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-10.text: Block after block, and still no floor. This march of reasons with nothing to land on is justification’s oldest crack: the regress.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-11.text: The chain of reasons can end in only three ways. The chain runs on for ever.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-12.text: The chain curls into a circle, each block leaning on the next. Or the chain lands on something that needs nothing beneath.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-14.text: So the digging stops. Foundationalists say a handful of basic beliefs hold themselves up, and the entire tower rests on those.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-15.text: Hit bedrock, and the question “why?” finally has nowhere left to go.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-00.text: Everyone says they want the truth. Almost nobody can say what the word means.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-01.text: Try it: when you call something true, what are you claiming?

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-02.text: Start with the world. Two hills and one lonely tree, sitting there being what they are.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-03.text: Whether or not anybody ever looks, draws, or argues about them.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-04.text: Back at the easel you sketch what you saw: two hills, one tree. That sketch is a claim about the land.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-05.text: Now, what would make it a good one?

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-07.text: You just used the oldest theory of truth. A belief is true when it matches how things are.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-08.text: Words on one side, world on the other, and truth is the fit. Philosophers call it correspondence.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-10.text: Fine, go and check. Hold the sketch up, look at the land, compare the two.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-11.text: Then somebody asks a rude little question: what are you comparing the sketch against?

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-13.text: One answer: stop hunting for a magic exit. A belief is true when it locks into everything else you hold — no contradictions, nothing left dangling.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-14.text: Truth is fitting the whole web.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-15.text: The other answer is blunter. A belief is true if it keeps working.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-16.text: It has to walk you across those real hills, year after year, and never once strand you. Comfort is not enough: only what survives the walk counts.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-00.text: You act. A moment later a question arrives on its own.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-02.text: You’re not alone in caring. Darwin traced empathy, fairness and care for your group back to instincts other animals have too.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-03.text: What you add is this: you stop and weigh the deed. You ask yourself “was that right?”

ethics-ethics-1/beat-04.text: Then you answer in reasons, on a balance no animal sets up.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-05.text: That inward weighing is your conscience. It tells you something’s wrong even when nobody’s watching.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-06.text: Where conscience comes from is disputed. Darwin says instinct, Freud says society turned inward, and Kant says reason itself.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-07.text: Aristotle asked a different question. Not which rules to follow, but what makes a life good.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-08.text: For Aristotle, what sets humans apart is reason.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-09.text: So living well means reasoning well, over a whole life.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-13.text: Aristotle’s word for the goal is eudaimonia. It usually gets translated as happiness, which is wrong.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-14.text: Flourishing is closer. Living and acting well, with a strong character, over a whole life.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-00.text: You’re walking past a shallow pond in good shoes. There’s a small child face-down in it, and nobody else anywhere.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-01.text: Nobody deliberates. You do not price the shoes against the child.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-02.text: There’s no comparison to make. Peter Singer’s whole argument starts from the fact that you already know this.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-03.text: So you’re in the water, shoes and all. Now Singer asks the awkward question: which part of that reasoning was about the child being near you?

ethics-ethics-10/beat-05.text: There’s another child. Same danger, same small cost to you, nine thousand kilometres further off.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-06.text: The argument that got you into the pond doesn’t obviously stop at the bank. Effective altruism started right there.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-00.text: Suppose happiness came in coins. Every pleasure you’ve ever had, poured onto one table and counted out like loose change.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-01.text: Jeremy Bentham built that table. A bar game, a helping of dessert, a symphony.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-02.text: The three pleasures are drawn the same size. To him they’re the same stuff.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-03.text: Bentham’s felicific calculus scored each for intensity, duration, certainty and reach, then added them up. He said push-pin is as good as poetry if the totals come out the same.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-04.text: Then his own student refused the arithmetic. Watch a second shelf go up above the table.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-05.text: John Stuart Mill would not leave a bar game and a symphony on one level.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-09.text: Two levels now, and the column below can no longer settle it. Mill’s test is not the size of the total but the verdict of people who have tasted both.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-00.text: Before you act, ask one question — what if everyone did this? Kant thought that single test could sort right from wrong, with no arithmetic at all.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-01.text: You need money, so you say “I promise to repay”, knowing full well you can’t. That private reason for acting is what Kant calls your maxim.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-02.text: Kant never asks what the act costs you. He asks whether your rule could be a law that everyone follows.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-03.text: So hand the rule to the whole world and run it.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-05.text: Now everyone breaks a promise the moment it suits them. Nobody believes one any more, so the word goes blank on every card.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-06.text: There’s no promising left to break.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-00.text: Rules and outcomes judge the act. Aristotle judges the person, and asks how much of a trait they have, not whether they followed anything.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-01.text: Too little fear-handling and you’re a coward: you run from things that should be faced. That’s one end of the rail.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-02.text: Too much and you’re reckless: you charge at things that should be walked away from. Same trait, other end, and it is a vice too.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-04.text: So courage is somewhere along here, and notice what kind of answer that is. Not a rule to write down, but an amount judged against what’s in front of you.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-00.text: No laws, no police, nothing above you at all. Every liberty you have is yours to keep.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-02.text: That last sentence is the whole problem. The case for leaving is not that freedom is bad.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-03.text: The case is that everyone else has freedom too.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-04.text: So you put part of what you hold into a wall, and everyone does the same. What comes back over it is order.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-05.text: Locke leaves a door in the wall. If what’s behind it turns on you, the deal is void and you may walk out.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-00.text: Here’s a plain report of what happened. You stole that money.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-01.text: Anyone can hold the sentence up against the world and check.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-02.text: Now the same report with a moral word in it. You acted wrongly in stealing that money.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-04.text: That’s emotivism. The extra word carries no extra fact.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-05.text: It’s a tone of voice, a wince set down in ink.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-07.text: Realists say the instrument is the problem. If cruelty really is wrong, that’s a fact about cruelty.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-08.text: A scale that cannot weigh it is a poor scale.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-00.text: A knife at your back, and you hand over the wallet. Nobody has ever thought you did that freely.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-01.text: A week later you hand a friend the same notes, repaying a loan. Same hand, same money, same causes running back forever.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-02.text: A hard determinist says neither one was free. The chain above your head is the same both times, so nothing under it can be different.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-04.text: Hume keeps a smaller kind of freedom. You act freely when you do what you want and nobody is holding your arm.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-00.text: A man at your door asks where your friend is hiding. He means to kill him.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-02.text: Kant’s answer looks monstrous, and he knew it. His reason is not that lying is ugly.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-03.text: Kant’s reason is that lying cannot be made a rule for all.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-04.text: So run his test. Write down what you are about to do, and hand a copy to everybody.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-05.text: Watch the bar. A lie only works on somebody expecting the truth, and now nobody is.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-08.text: Constant pushed back at once. Tell the truth and your friend dies, so the blood is on your hands.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-00.text: A pig can be frightened, and can be hurt, and would rather not be. The question is whether any of that puts it inside ethics or leaves it outside.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-01.text: For most of history the line ran here. The reason given was reason itself.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-02.text: Animals cannot argue, cannot promise, and cannot be held to anything. So they were furniture.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-03.text: But look at what else that test catches. Infants cannot reason.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-04.text: Nor can someone deeply cognitively impaired. Nobody thinks they’re outside, so that’s not the real test.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-06.text: Change the test to the one people actually use, and nobody has to argue about where the line goes. It moves by itself, and it takes the pig with it.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-00.text: Four decisions, all about the same life. Yours.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-01.text: Now watch the last column. Somebody has signed three of them off on your behalf, for your own good.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-02.text: Mill thought there was one honest test, and it’s the middle column. Not how risky the choice is.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-05.text: Three of these signatures were not written freely. The fourth one was.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-07.text: The rule is easy while the choices are small. It gets expensive at the end of a life.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-00.text: You find a wallet on the pavement. Now what?

ethics-ethics-2/beat-01.text: One small choice is about to get three different verdicts.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-02.text: Ethics hands you three lenses. One asks what happens next.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-03.text: One asks what your duty is. One asks who the act turns you into.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-04.text: Most people use all three without noticing.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-05.text: Mill points the first lens at the wallet. Did handing it in make anyone’s life go better?

ethics-ethics-2/beat-06.text: For him that’s the whole question, and everybody’s happiness counts the same.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-08.text: Kant ignores the happy ending. He says to act only on a rule you could want everyone to follow.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-09.text: Try Kant’s test on the rule “keep any wallet you find”. It eats itself, because nobody would hand one in.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-10.text: Aristotle asks a third question. Not what to do, but who you’re becoming.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-11.text: Every honest act makes the next one easier. That’s what he means by a good life.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-00.text: Seven harms, all the same size. The only difference is when each one happens.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-01.text: Every government discounts the far harms first. A cost two hundred years out is written down until almost nothing is left.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-02.text: Some of that is fair. A distant benefit is less certain, and the people there may be richer than you.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-03.text: But strip those reasons out and something is left. A rate applied to the date itself.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-05.text: Here’s what was under it the whole time. Seven people, none of whom chose which century to be born in.
