ethics-ethics-21/beat-00.text: A doctor gives enough morphine to stop the pain. Everyone knows it will also shorten the life.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-01.text: Two outcomes, both certain, both from one act. Only one of them was the point.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-02.text: Aquinas saw that you judge the two arrows in different ways. So does everyone, not just in hospitals.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-04.text: Now the case that tests it. Same two outcomes, except the death is how the relief is achieved.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-05.text: The doctrine says that one is different. You may accept a harm alongside your aim.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-06.text: You may not walk through it.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-00.text: Five things people say they want out of a life, in no particular order. In a moment somebody offers you all five at once.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-01.text: Now the offer. A tank, a lifetime of experience indistinguishable from the real thing, and no way back.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-02.text: Almost everybody says no, and most can’t say why. The reason is in the picture.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-04.text: One cable, into one column. The other four are not switched off.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-07.text: That refusal is evidence about you. If pleasure were all that mattered, the tank would be an easy yes.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-00.text: You pass a shallow pond and a small child is drowning in it. Wading in ruins an expensive pair of shoes.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-01.text: Nobody thinks this is a hard question.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-02.text: So the first gauge goes straight to the top, and it doesn’t even feel like a moral decision. It feels like noticing.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-03.text: Now the second child, dying of something preventable, eight thousand miles off. The same money, the same certainty, the same small cost to you.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-05.text: Singer asks what could hold the second gauge down. Not the cost, which is the same.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-06.text: Not your power to help, which is the same. Only how far away it is, and distance is not a moral property.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-00.text: A sentence, and the four things people say it’s for. In an ordinary case all four agree, so nobody has to choose.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-01.text: Stop him doing it again. Stop others copying him.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-02.text: Make him better. Give him what he has coming.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-03.text: Now a man of ninety, forty years after the crime, ill and harmless. He won’t reoffend, and nobody is watching.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-04.text: Three of the four pillars have nothing left to hold. The sentence hasn’t stopped feeling right.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-07.text: The other side runs the same trick backwards, and that reply is why nobody holds deterrence on its own.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-00.text: Somebody stopped you for your own good. Ask whether they had the right.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-01.text: John Stuart Mill drew the line in one sentence, and it’s narrower than it sounds.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-01.text: A realist hears a plain fact, true whether or not anybody agrees.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-03.text: An expressivist hears a cry of disgust, wearing the grammar of a statement.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-05.text: A. J. Ayer went furthest. For him, a moral sentence vents an attitude and is neither true nor false.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-07.text: Each reading costs something, and the bill falls due when two moralities collide.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-00.text: Your principle says yes. Your gut says no, and says it loudly.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-01.text: A principle says “always maximise happiness”. A judgement about a case says “framing an innocent man is monstrous”.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-02.text: Sometimes the two collide. One of them has to move, and the argument is about which.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-05.text: Many obvious feelings turned out to be prejudice. Many elegant rules turned out to be too clean.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-07.text: The aim is a web that holds together. Nothing in it is the unshakeable floor.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-00.text: A soldier throws himself onto a grenade and saves his squad. Everybody calls it heroic.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-02.text: The gap between those two answers has a name. A supererogatory act is good and not required.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-01.text: Three verdicts. Same dilemma, same goal, yet they split.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-02.text: A runaway trolley hurtles towards five people on the track. Your hand rests on a lever.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-03.text: Pull it, and the trolley swerves onto a side track, where one person stands instead.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-04.text: Pull the lever, do nothing, or search for another way? Three great theories answer the same question — what makes an action good?

ethics-ethics-3/beat-05.text: John Stuart Mill would pull. For him, the right act promotes the most happiness, counting each person equally.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-06.text: Five lives saved outweigh one lost. People who judge an act this way are called utilitarians.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-07.text: Immanuel Kant would not. He won’t trade lives like sums, because the one person has a worth no arithmetic can outweigh.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-08.text: Duty binds whatever follows from it.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-09.text: Aristotle asks a different question. Not what you should do, but who you become.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-10.text: What would a person of practical wisdom do here?

ethics-ethics-30/beat-00.text: You’ve met the great theories. The question now is how to live with all three of them.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-01.text: Consequentialism judges an act by what it brings about. Ask what the outcomes will be.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-02.text: Deontology judges by duties and rights. Ask which rules are at stake and who’s owed what.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-03.text: Virtue ethics asks about character. What would a good person do, and who are you becoming?

ethics-ethics-30/beat-05.text: A colleague is secretly cheating customers. Weigh the harm of silence against the fallout of speaking.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-07.text: Often the three lenses agree. Sometimes they point three different ways, and no formula breaks the tie.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-00.text: Something is on a shelf and you’ve been told to fetch it. The duty is lit, and at this point nobody has asked whether you can.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-01.text: A ladder appears, so you climb. Four rungs, and the shelf is closer.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-02.text: Nothing about the duty has changed because nothing needed to.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-03.text: The ladder ends. You stretch as far as you can, and the shelf is still above your hand.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-06.text: Now extend the ladder. The lamp comes straight back on, and you did not become a better person in between.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-07.text: The duty was tracking the reach the whole time.

ethics-ethics-32/beat-00.text: One of these two has thought about a hard moral question for years. The other has just asked them what the answer is.

ethics-ethics-32/beat-01.text: Behind the verdict sit the reasons: the cases weighed, the objections met, the times they changed their mind. The card is only the last line of it.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-01.text: Now one speaker says four words: “I promise I will.”

ethics-ethics-37/beat-02.text: Watch the cord appear between the two.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-00.text: Cultures disagree about right and wrong. That much is just a fact.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-01.text: Saying there’s no right answer underneath the disagreement is a much bigger claim, and a separate one.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-02.text: First the harmless fact. Societies do hold different codes.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-03.text: The bold claim, called moral relativism, goes further. Whether something is right depends on the group asking, and there’s no answer underneath.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-04.text: Sliding from the first to the second is the classic mistake.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-07.text: The objectivist fires back: some truths hold whatever a culture says. Torturing a child for fun is wrong, full stop.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-08.text: Cultures differing does not make every code equally true.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-10.text: Returning a favour. Bans on murder and incest.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-11.text: A shared floor, under the feet of cultures sure they stood apart.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-00.text: You promised a dying friend you’d burn his letters. Nobody else heard it.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-01.text: A month later the promise is still there, and he is not.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-02.text: Break the promise and name the person who’s worse off. The naming is the hard part.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-05.text: Countries with opt-out organ donation get far more donors than countries with opt-in.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-07.text: The form takes the same ten seconds either way. Only the resting answer changed.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-00.text: In Greece, in India, in China, humans began to argue about how to live. Out loud, for the first time.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-01.text: Karl Jaspers gave that window a name: the Axial Age. Three places, no contact between them, all starting to ask the same kind of question.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-02.text: Nobody has ever agreed on why.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-03.text: Socrates never wrote a word down. What survives of him was written later, by a student.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-04.text: In Athens, he walked up to people and asked them what virtue was. The city put him on trial and killed him for it.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-06.text: China’s word is ren, something like humaneness. Confucius says it grows only between people.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-00.text: Five lives saved. So why does this one feel wrong?

ethics-ethics-6/beat-01.text: Same numbers, different hands — your gut splits where the math does not.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-02.text: Earlier you met the lever: divert the trolley, one dies instead of five. Philosophers then twisted it, each version keeping the five-for-one math but changing how the one dies.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-03.text: Thomson’s 1985 twist: you stand on a bridge beside a large stranger. Shove him onto the track and his body stops the trolley, saving five.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-04.text: Most who would pull the lever refuse to push.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-05.text: The arithmetic is identical — five lives for one, which is all a utilitarian counts. Yet the switch and the shove split people.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-06.text: For Foot, diverting redirects a threat. Shoving makes a person your instrument.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-00.text: Two drivers glance at their phone for exactly two seconds. One gets home, eats dinner, forgets it.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-01.text: The other is in a courtroom by Friday. Same two seconds.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-02.text: Here’s the first driver. Empty road, nothing ahead.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-03.text: The driver looks down, looks up, and the road is as she left it. She parks and never thinks about it again.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-04.text: Here’s the second driver. Same phone, same road, same two seconds.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-05.text: The only difference: on his stretch of road, a child is already stepping out.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-06.text: Freeze both cars and compare the two seconds. Same phone, same speed, same shrug about the risk.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-07.text: Nothing inside the drivers is different at all. Only the road is.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-09.text: Now let luck in. On road B the child is there.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-10.text: That driver will stand trial for a death. The other drives home and never even learns she took a risk.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-12.text: In 1976 Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel named this clash: moral luck. Whether you end up decent or criminal depends partly on which road you happened to take.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-13.text: Nagel stated the intuition people keep breaking.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-00.text: A friend goes quiet for two weeks. You could work out what you owe them, fairly and impartially.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-01.text: Or you could just go and sit with them. For a long time, only the first one counted as ethics.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-02.text: Most big theories start the same way. Step back, be impartial, and find the rule or the total that covers everyone equally.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-03.text: Tidy boxes, with nobody’s name in any of them.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-04.text: Then you look up. Someone is on the floor by their bed, and no box fits them.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-05.text: Not a case, not a number. The one you know.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-06.text: You cross the room and get down beside them. No theory has said a word yet.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-07.text: Something else is already telling you what to do.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-09.text: That move has a name. Carol Gilligan kept hearing people reason through bonds and care, and the textbooks had no word for it.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-10.text: Gilligan called the pattern a different voice.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-13.text: Nel Noddings built care into a full ethics. For her, morality grows out of the bond between the one caring and the one cared for.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-14.text: You learned right and wrong on a kitchen floor, long before any rulebook.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-15.text: Critics feared care would trap people in endless self-sacrifice. Gilligan’s answer: care and justice are two lenses, not rivals.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-16.text: Rules stop you being cruel. Care notices the person the rules never mention.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-00.text: Most hard choices have a right answer buried in them somewhere. Some do not.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-01.text: Some leave a mark on you whichever way you go.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-02.text: In 1940 a student came to Sartre. His brother had been killed by the Germans and he wanted to fight.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-03.text: The student’s mother lived for him alone, and his leaving would break her.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-04.text: Neither claim outranks the other. This is a dilemma, not a hard sum, because there is no scale both of them fit on.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-06.text: The student goes. Say he was right to, as most people think he was.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-07.text: Now look at the board: the other claim has not moved. Nothing about his choice removed it.

logic-arguments-1/beat-01.text: Watch closely. Not how loud the voices get, but what the words say.

logic-arguments-1/beat-02.text: Shouting back is not a counter-argument. A raised voice is the same noise aimed the other way.

logic-arguments-1/beat-03.text: Three rounds in. Not one reason has been given by either of them.

logic-arguments-1/beat-04.text: Most people picture a shouting match when they hear the word “argument”.

logic-arguments-1/beat-05.text: That’s a quarrel. And a quarrel has no way to end, only a way to get louder.

logic-arguments-1/beat-06.text: Philosophy means something else by the word. An argument is a machine with parts.

logic-arguments-1/beat-07.text: Reasons, called premises, offered in support of a conclusion. That’s the whole machine.

logic-arguments-1/beat-09.text: Aristotle was the first to write the machine down, around 350 BCE.

logic-arguments-1/beat-10.text: Grant him the two premises and the conclusion follows whether you like it or not. No volume required.

logic-arguments-1/beat-12.text: Volume is not a reason. That’s worth saying plainly, because almost everyone behaves as though the opposite were true.

logic-arguments-1/beat-14.text: Schopenhauer saw that people argue with two very different aims.

logic-arguments-1/beat-15.text: One aim is to find out what’s true. The other is to win, and Schopenhauer catalogued thirty-eight tricks for winning when you’re in the wrong.

logic-arguments-1/beat-16.text: Socrates went the other way. On trial for his life, he answered his accuser with nothing but questions.

logic-arguments-1/beat-17.text: Socrates kept asking Meletus who improves the young, until Meletus contradicted himself in front of the whole court. Socrates never raised his voice, and never needed to.

logic-arguments-1/beat-18.text: So give the two fighters the same disagreement again, with reasons.

logic-arguments-1/beat-19.text: A premise is a claim you can go and check.

logic-arguments-1/beat-20.text: And here’s a real counter. It engages the reason instead of the person.

logic-arguments-1/beat-21.text: Same two people, same disagreement. Nobody threw a punch, and for the first time it can go somewhere.

logic-arguments-1/beat-22.text: Mill went further: you don’t fully understand your own position until you understand theirs.

logic-arguments-10/beat-00.text: A friend says “he is rich, so he must be happy”, and you nod along. Two sentences went past you, and a third one never did.

logic-arguments-10/beat-01.text: Nothing actually joins them. Being rich and being happy are different things, and the sentence tying one to the other was never said.

logic-arguments-10/beat-02.text: Logic has a name for an argument like this. An enthymeme: one that runs on a premise nobody says out loud.

logic-arguments-10/beat-03.text: There it is, sitting under the line.

logic-arguments-10/beat-05.text: So say the claim out loud. All rich people are happy.

logic-arguments-10/beat-06.text: Up it comes through the line, and once you can read the words you can see they’re rubbish.

logic-arguments-11/beat-00.text: A proof has to rest on something outside itself. Watch this proof stop doing so, without a single step going wrong.

logic-arguments-11/beat-01.text: Two claims go up. The book is God’s word, and whatever God says is true.

logic-arguments-11/beat-02.text: Innocent so far. Nothing has been smuggled in yet.

logic-arguments-11/beat-03.text: Step three answers the obvious objection, and step four draws the conclusion. The whole structure now stands on that line: evidence from outside the argument.

logic-arguments-11/beat-05.text: Now test the chain. Every link holds, step after step, nothing missing and nothing limping.

logic-arguments-11/beat-06.text: A chain that sound is what makes the trap dangerous.

logic-arguments-12/beat-00.text: Somebody says “you’re either with us or against us”. Two doors, and you’re told to pick one.

logic-arguments-12/beat-01.text: Both doors are real, and nothing here is made up. Some people are with you, and some are against you.

logic-arguments-12/beat-02.text: The trick is the claim that only two doors exist. Nobody argued for that claim.

logic-arguments-12/beat-03.text: You were put in a room with two doors.

logic-arguments-12/beat-05.text: Turn the lights on along the rest of the wall. Nothing was built just now: these doors were in the room before anyone made you an offer.

logic-arguments-13/beat-00.text: Let one student retake one quiz. That’s the whole proposal, and nobody in the room objects to it.

logic-arguments-14/beat-03.text: Something is smuggling false certainty through a form you trust every day. The form is not what went wrong.

logic-arguments-17/beat-08.text: One is a machine with parts you can inspect. The other is tipping over, because there was nothing under it.

logic-arguments-18/beat-00.text: One person says the water here is safe. You’ve no idea whether it is.

logic-arguments-18/beat-01.text: Now the whole town says the same thing. Every voice, loudly, and a few are upset with you for asking.

logic-arguments-18/beat-02.text: Here’s the machinery. The handle is what they turn.

logic-arguments-18/beat-03.text: The needle is whether the water is safe.

logic-arguments-18/beat-04.text: There’s a hole in the shaft. Nothing that happens on the left reaches the right.

logic-arguments-18/beat-06.text: Here’s the other kind of link. Somebody tested the water, and this shaft has no hole in it.

logic-arguments-19/beat-00.text: A rule, and four cards. Each one has a letter on the face and a number on the back.

logic-arguments-19/beat-01.text: Which two would you turn to test it? Almost everybody reaches for the vowel and the even number.

logic-arguments-19/beat-02.text: Turn the four and the rule survives whatever is on its back. A consonant is allowed an even number.

logic-arguments-19/beat-04.text: There it is. A vowel behind the seven and the rule is dead on the table.

logic-arguments-19/beat-05.text: You went looking for the card that would say yes. Only the card that can say no is really a test.

logic-arguments-2/beat-00.text: A master builder sets the first stone.

logic-arguments-2/beat-01.text: Every argument hides the same skeleton. Learn to see it once, and you read minds forever.

logic-arguments-2/beat-02.text: Two stones below. One resting on top.

logic-arguments-2/beat-03.text: That shape is every argument you’ll ever meet.

logic-arguments-2/beat-04.text: The two stones at the base are the premises — the reasons you lay down. Words like “because” and “since” point them out.

logic-arguments-2/beat-05.text: The stone on top is the conclusion. Aristotle called it the claim that must follow.

logic-arguments-2/beat-06.text: The words “therefore”, “so” and “thus” all flag a conclusion.

logic-arguments-2/beat-08.text: Here’s logic’s oldest structure, first written down around 350 BCE.

logic-arguments-2/beat-09.text: Grant the builder both premises, and no matter how you feel, the top stone is forced into place. That’s what the phrase “follows of necessity” means.

logic-arguments-2/beat-11.text: Pull the reasons and nothing holds the claim up. Premises aren’t decoration but the load-bearing part.

logic-arguments-20/beat-00.text: Three versions of the same claim. Nobody has lied and nobody has invented anything.

logic-arguments-20/beat-01.text: What differs is the support underneath. One version kept all of it.

logic-arguments-20/beat-02.text: One kept some. One is standing on a single leg.

logic-arguments-20/beat-03.text: A straw man is not usually a lie. It’s repeating the weakest version you heard and then arguing with that.

logic-arguments-20/beat-05.text: Down it goes, and the real argument hasn’t moved an inch.

logic-arguments-20/beat-06.text: The repair has a name. Build the strongest version they could have meant, and take that one on instead.

logic-arguments-21/beat-00.text: Four things that have something to do with a fire starting. Only one of them is the fire.

logic-arguments-21/beat-01.text: Two tests, and they ask different questions. Take a thing away, and see if the fire still starts.

logic-arguments-21/beat-02.text: Then try that thing alone, and see if it starts the fire.

logic-arguments-21/beat-03.text: A match in petrol lights it every time, and a spark would have done just as well. Enough, but not required.

logic-arguments-21/beat-05.text: It being Tuesday fails both tests. Fuel and heat and oxygen together pass both.

logic-arguments-21/beat-06.text: So there are four boxes, not two. Most arguments that go wrong here have put something in the wrong one.

logic-arguments-22/beat-00.text: For two thousand years the claim “all swans are white” held up. Then someone sailed to Australia and saw a black one, and that was the end of it.

logic-arguments-22/beat-01.text: Aristotle boiled talk about groups down to four shapes: all, none, some, and some-not. Here’s the first one, with the group it’s about underneath.

logic-arguments-22/beat-02.text: A universal claim is a promise about every single member. The promise is worth a lot and breaks easily, because one exception breaks all of it.

logic-arguments-22/beat-04.text: One cat is not black, and that alone finishes the claim. The other seventeen don’t help it in the slightest.

logic-arguments-23/beat-00.text: Four small words carry every argument you’ll ever check. Start with two.

logic-arguments-23/beat-01.text: P and Q are either true or false. Four rows cover every way that can go.

logic-arguments-23/beat-02.text: Take the word “or”. In speech it often means one or the other, but in logic it means at least one.

logic-arguments-23/beat-03.text: So taking both cake and pie isn’t cheating. It’s the plainest way to keep the promise.

logic-arguments-23/beat-05.text: Now the awkward one. The sentence “if P, then Q” is a promise about what follows P.

logic-arguments-23/beat-06.text: It breaks in one place only: P happens and Q does not.

logic-arguments-23/beat-08.text: When P never happens, the promise was never called on. Nothing was broken.

logic-arguments-24/beat-00.text: Sherlock Holmes never deduced anything. He guessed, brilliantly.

logic-arguments-24/beat-01.text: Deduction runs from a rule to a conclusion that can’t be false.

logic-arguments-24/beat-02.text: Induction runs from many cases to a rule that’s probably right.

logic-arguments-24/beat-03.text: Abduction runs from what you see to the likeliest reason you’re seeing it.

logic-arguments-24/beat-05.text: Look at what comes out. Deduction hands back the shape you fed it.

logic-arguments-24/beat-07.text: That certainty has a price. A guaranteed conclusion tells you nothing new.

logic-arguments-25/beat-00.text: A test that’s ninety-nine per cent accurate says you have a disease. Almost everyone reads that as “almost certainly ill”.

logic-arguments-25/beat-02.text: The disease hits one person in ten thousand. So take ten thousand people and run the test on all of them, and just count what comes out.

logic-arguments-25/beat-03.text: One person in the crowd is actually ill, and the test almost certainly catches them. There they are, a bar one unit wide.

logic-arguments-25/beat-05.text: But one per cent of everyone else tests positive too. One per cent of a big number is a big number: a hundred people get the same letter you did.

logic-arguments-26/beat-00.text: Here’s a strange way to prove something is true. Begin by assuming it is false.

logic-arguments-26/beat-01.text: Then be as reasonable as you possibly can.

logic-arguments-26/beat-02.text: Suppose there’s a largest number. Call it N.

logic-arguments-26/beat-03.text: Nothing wrong with supposing it. That’s the whole move, and you’re allowed to suppose anything at all.

logic-arguments-26/beat-04.text: Now just follow it. N plus one is a number, and it’s bigger than N.

logic-arguments-26/beat-05.text: So N is not the largest after all. That’s flatly at odds with what you assumed.

logic-arguments-26/beat-07.text: Something in that chain has to give. Every step after the first was valid, so the break lands where it started.

logic-arguments-26/beat-08.text: The assumption was false. There’s no largest number.

logic-arguments-27/beat-00.text: Read the card, then try to decide whether it’s telling the truth.

logic-arguments-27/beat-01.text: Suppose the card speaks true. Then what it says holds, and the card is false.

logic-arguments-27/beat-02.text: Suppose the card speaks false. Then what it says is wrong, and the card is true.

logic-arguments-27/beat-03.text: The culprit is the pointing. An ordinary sentence describes the world, but this one describes itself.

logic-arguments-27/beat-05.text: Epimenides said it first, and he was a Cretan calling all Cretans liars.

logic-arguments-27/beat-07.text: Russell hit the same wall in set theory, and Kurt Gödel turned the trick into a theorem.

logic-arguments-28/beat-00.text: Every big argument hides one small claim. It says two cases are alike, so treat them alike.

logic-arguments-28/beat-01.text: An analogy is inductive. Never certain, often strong, and only as good as the likeness it rests on.

logic-arguments-28/beat-02.text: Strong means many likenesses that bear on the conclusion. Weak means the likeness is only skin deep.

logic-arguments-28/beat-03.text: One difference that matters can sink the whole argument. The name for it is a disanalogy.

logic-arguments-28/beat-05.text: Judith Jarvis Thomson imagines you waking up wired to a famous violinist who needs your kidneys.

logic-arguments-28/beat-07.text: Somebody argues that banning hate speech is fine because shouting fire in a theatre is banned.

logic-arguments-29/beat-00.text: A china teapot orbits the sun, between Earth and Mars. Prove it doesn’t.

logic-arguments-29/beat-01.text: You cannot. Bertrand Russell picked the example because nobody could, and that settles nothing.

logic-arguments-29/beat-02.text: The burden of proof is the job of backing a claim up. It falls on whoever asserts.

logic-arguments-29/beat-03.text: Before anybody has argued, the beam is empty. Withholding belief is the resting state.

logic-arguments-29/beat-05.text: Somebody keeps an invisible dragon in the garage. Every test you propose is explained away.

logic-arguments-29/beat-07.text: Sagan argues that a dragon no test can reach is the same picture as an empty garage.

logic-arguments-3/beat-00.text: A perfectly logical argument can still be dead wrong. Flawless structure isn’t enough without true premises.

logic-arguments-3/beat-01.text: Two tests, and never confuse them. An argument is valid when its shape won’t let true premises lead to a false conclusion.

logic-arguments-3/beat-02.text: An argument is sound when it’s valid and the premises are actually true.

logic-arguments-3/beat-03.text: All toasters are gold. All gold things are time machines.

logic-arguments-3/beat-04.text: So all toasters are time machines. The form is flawless, which makes the argument valid.

logic-arguments-3/beat-05.text: Yet the conclusion is false because the premises are. Valid form, false premises: the argument is valid but not sound.

logic-arguments-3/beat-08.text: Validity tests the form, and soundness tests form and facts. To resist a valid argument, you can’t attack the logic, so you must reject a premise.

logic-arguments-30/beat-00.text: You’ve spent a whole path taking arguments apart. Now build one on purpose.

logic-arguments-30/beat-01.text: Start from the conclusion you mean to defend. Then find the premises that would force it.

logic-arguments-30/beat-02.text: Drag every hidden assumption into the open. An argument leaning on an unstated one is leaning on nothing.

logic-arguments-30/beat-03.text: Check the form holds, and only then check whether each premise is true.

logic-arguments-30/beat-05.text: Now turn on your own work. Where is the weakest premise, and what would a critic aim at?

logic-arguments-30/beat-07.text: Steelman the objection before anybody else makes it. Build the strongest version and answer that one.

logic-arguments-31/beat-00.text: A fair coin, an ordinary table, and nothing up anyone's sleeve. Watch the run build and watch what your gut starts telling you.

logic-arguments-31/beat-02.text: The needle underneath is the actual chance of heads on the next flip, and it has not moved.

logic-arguments-31/beat-03.text: Now the feeling is loud, and it says tails is due. Every part of you is certain the coin owes you one.

logic-arguments-31/beat-06.text: In 1913 a Monte Carlo wheel came up black twenty-six times running. Players lost fortunes betting on red, each one certain it was overdue.

logic-arguments-31/beat-07.text: The wheel had no idea what it had been doing.

logic-arguments-32/beat-00.text: Two people, one question, and no way out of it. Watch what happens to the second person whichever way they answer.

logic-arguments-32/beat-01.text: The question is “have you stopped cheating at cards?” It sounds like an ordinary yes-or-no, and is not one.

logic-arguments-32/beat-02.text: Try yes. Yes, you stopped, which means you were cheating before.

logic-arguments-32/beat-03.text: The accusation now stands on the record. Nobody ever made it.

logic-arguments-32/beat-04.text: Try no, which feels like the safe one. No, you haven’t stopped, so you are cheating right now.

logic-arguments-33/beat-00.text: Seven measurements, and a straight line drawn through them. It misses most of the dots and nobody is pretending otherwise.

logic-arguments-33/beat-01.text: Give the line a couple of bends and the line starts to behave. Now the line runs near every dot, and still looks like a finding.

logic-arguments-33/beat-02.text: Keep going and you can thread every single dot exactly. Perfect fit.

logic-arguments-33/beat-03.text: Nothing left over, and no measurement unexplained.

logic-arguments-33/beat-04.text: Then a new measurement comes in, and the perfect curve is nowhere near it. It was never learning the pattern.

logic-arguments-33/beat-05.text: It was learning your seven dots, errors and all.

logic-arguments-33/beat-08.text: That’s what the razor is really for. Between two accounts that fit the evidence equally, take the one with fewer parts.

logic-arguments-33/beat-09.text: Every extra part is another thing that can be wrong.

logic-arguments-34/beat-00.text: A jar of marbles, and you want to know what fraction are dark. The dashed line is the true answer, and you’re not allowed to look at it.

logic-arguments-34/beat-01.text: So you pull a handful. Your estimate is the solid line and the bracket around it is how wrong you might be.

logic-arguments-34/beat-03.text: Pull more and the bracket closes fast. This part feels like progress, and it’s the part everybody remembers about sample size.

logic-arguments-34/beat-04.text: Then it stops paying. Four times the marbles only halves the bracket.

logic-arguments-34/beat-05.text: Error falls with the square root of the count, not in step with it.

logic-arguments-34/beat-08.text: Now the awkward one. Here’s a huge sample, drawn only from people who answered the phone.

logic-arguments-34/beat-09.text: The bracket is tight around the wrong number.

logic-arguments-35/beat-00.text: Two things, measured all summer. Watch the two columns climb.

logic-arguments-35/beat-01.text: Ice cream sales climb. Drownings climb with them, week for week.

logic-arguments-35/beat-02.text: The shape is real and it’s not a coincidence.

logic-arguments-35/beat-03.text: So here’s the arrow everybody draws. It says cones cause drownings.

logic-arguments-35/beat-04.text: Nobody believes it, and the data doesn’t care what you believe.

logic-arguments-35/beat-06.text: A cause under both is called a confounder. Take the summer out and the link between cone and drowning vanishes.

logic-arguments-35/beat-09.text: The link is rarely this obvious. Children with bigger feet read better, and the whole cause is age.

logic-arguments-35/beat-10.text: Coffee looked deadly for years because smokers drank coffee.

logic-arguments-36/beat-00.text: Somebody claims there’s an elephant in this room. Here’s the room, marked out in squares.

logic-arguments-36/beat-02.text: So the rule. Finding nothing counts for as much as the chance your search would have found the thing, had it been there.

logic-arguments-36/beat-03.text: Look in two squares of a forest for one beetle and the empty result tells you almost nothing. The forest is large and the beetle is small.

logic-arguments-36/beat-06.text: This is why the famous line is only half true. The saying “absence of evidence is not evidence of absence” describes a bad search and nothing else.

logic-arguments-36/beat-07.text: Used on a careful search, it’s a way of ignoring a result. Say the words out loud and then ask how hard anybody looked.

logic-arguments-37/beat-00.text: A village with one barber and one rule. He shaves every man who doesn’t shave himself, and nobody else.

logic-arguments-37/beat-01.text: It sorts the whole village without an argument. Shave yourself and he leaves you alone.

logic-arguments-37/beat-04.text: That’s the whole result, and the result bites harder than you would think. A sentence can be built perfectly and still describe nothing that could exist.

logic-arguments-37/beat-05.text: Russell found the real one in 1901. Take the set of all sets that do not contain themselves.

logic-arguments-37/beat-09.text: Frege had a volume at the printer. He added an appendix saying the ground had gone, and published it anyway.

logic-arguments-38/beat-00.text: An argument is a shape. Three steps, stacked, and a word goes in at the top.

logic-arguments-38/beat-01.text: Anselm feeds in the word God, “that than which nothing greater can be conceived”. For him, existing is greater than not existing.

logic-arguments-38/beat-02.text: A monk named Gaunilo built the same mill and changed one word. He fed in the island than which no greater island can be conceived.

logic-arguments-38/beat-04.text: Look at the two frames again. Not one glyph differs between them.

logic-arguments-38/beat-05.text: So whatever is wrong is wrong in both, and it was there before anybody mentioned an island.

logic-arguments-39/beat-00.text: Most claims need evidence before you can argue with them. A few need nothing but themselves.

logic-arguments-39/beat-01.text: Three claims, one to a plank. The test is to hold each one to the standard it sets.

logic-arguments-39/beat-03.text: The sentence “nothing can be proved” is itself a claim, so it invites the one question it forbids.

logic-arguments-39/beat-04.text: Prove it, and something can be proved. Don’t, and you’re asking to be believed on nothing.

logic-arguments-39/beat-05.text: No outside evidence went into the verdict. The sentence did the whole job.

logic-arguments-4/beat-00.text: Some arguments prove their point. Others only make it a good bet.

logic-arguments-4/beat-01.text: Both are useful, and grading one by the other’s standard is where people go wrong.

logic-arguments-4/beat-02.text: A deductive argument aims to guarantee. Grade the argument valid, or sound.

logic-arguments-4/beat-03.text: An inductive argument only makes its conclusion likely, so grade it strong or weak. Use the wrong ruler and you get the wrong verdict.

logic-arguments-4/beat-04.text: Take “all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, so he’s mortal”. Grant the first two and the third can’t be false.

logic-arguments-4/beat-05.text: The needle pins and the guarantee locks shut.

logic-arguments-4/beat-06.text: Now take “most Greeks eat olives, Socrates is Greek, so he eats olives”. He might hate them, so the conclusion is only probable.

logic-arguments-4/beat-07.text: The needle slips off certainty and the dice come out.

logic-arguments-40/beat-00.text: Every emerald anybody has ever checked came out green.

logic-arguments-40/beat-01.text: A great many stones, and every one of them says the same thing.

logic-arguments-40/beat-02.text: Now a new word. A stone is grue if it looks green when checked before tonight.

logic-arguments-40/beat-03.text: Nobody has checked one after tonight. So every stone on record is grue as well.

logic-arguments-40/beat-05.text: Pull a fresh stone out tomorrow and green calls it green. Grue calls it blue.

logic-arguments-40/beat-07.text: Green looks simpler. But simple depends on which words you started with.

logic-arguments-41/beat-00.text: Linda is thirty-one, outspoken, and studied philosophy at university.

logic-arguments-41/beat-01.text: Is she more likely to be a bank teller, or a bank teller who’s also an activist?

logic-arguments-41/beat-02.text: Most people pick the second. The extra detail fits Linda.

logic-arguments-41/beat-03.text: But every activist teller is a teller. The second group sits inside the first.

logic-arguments-41/beat-05.text: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman found this in nine of ten people, including statisticians.

logic-arguments-41/beat-07.text: Adding a detail narrows a claim. Narrower means fewer people fit it.

logic-arguments-5/beat-00.text: A proof is a chain: premises that march, step by step, to a conclusion. One weak link, and it falls.

logic-arguments-5/beat-01.text: An argument moves from premises, the claims you grant, to a conclusion they force. Each move is an inference.

logic-arguments-5/beat-02.text: Feed the premises in, and the conclusion comes out the other end.

logic-arguments-5/beat-03.text: Euclid’s circles around point A and point B cross at C, each through the other’s centre. Line AB equals line AC and line BC, so line AC equals line BC.

logic-arguments-5/beat-04.text: A triangle, proved link by link.

logic-arguments-5/beat-07.text: Validity lives in the form, not the vibe. Spell out every inference to see where the chain might break, and climb from the simplest step up.

logic-arguments-6/beat-00.text: Two tiny words run almost every argument. Master the words “if” and “then”, and you hold logic’s favourite tool.

logic-arguments-6/beat-01.text: A conditional says “if P, then Q”. P is the antecedent — the condition.

logic-arguments-6/beat-02.text: Q is the consequent — what follows. The sentence promises nothing about P alone, only the link between them.

logic-arguments-6/beat-03.text: Take the sentence “if it rains, the streets get wet”. Nothing in it says rain is falling right now.

logic-arguments-6/beat-04.text: The sentence claims only a link: if rain comes, wet streets follow. A sunny day leaves the promise unbroken.

logic-arguments-7/beat-00.text: There are two moves that can never let you down. Learn them, and no one can slide a broken argument past you again.

logic-arguments-7/beat-01.text: Start with a rule you already believe. If it rains, the streets get wet.

logic-arguments-7/beat-02.text: Nothing clever yet. Just a promise: whenever the first thing happens, so does the second.

logic-arguments-7/beat-03.text: Now add one fact. You glance outside and rain is falling.

logic-arguments-7/beat-04.text: Watch what that single fact unlocks.

logic-arguments-7/beat-06.text: That’s the first move, and it has a name: modus ponens. Say the “if” part is true, and the “then” part comes free.

logic-arguments-7/beat-07.text: You proved something about the street without looking at it.

logic-arguments-7/beat-08.text: Same rule, new day. This time you ignore the sky and check the street.

logic-arguments-7/beat-11.text: That’s the second move: modus tollens. Knock out the “then” part, and the “if” part falls with it.

logic-arguments-7/beat-12.text: You just read the sky by looking at the pavement.

logic-arguments-8/beat-00.text: You’re almost home when the pavement registers a beat late. Behind you the street is dark and soaking, and your head has already answered why.

logic-arguments-8/beat-02.text: You walk back to the wet patch. The rule is one you’d bet money on: if it rains, the streets get wet.

logic-arguments-8/beat-03.text: And tonight these streets are definitely wet.

logic-arguments-8/beat-04.text: So you run the rule backwards. Streets wet, therefore rain.

logic-arguments-8/beat-05.text: It feels like the same reliable move you used yesterday, only read from the other end.

logic-arguments-8/beat-07.text: Twenty steps on, you hear it. A sprinkler, sweeping the pavement from next door’s lawn, and it’s been going all evening.

logic-arguments-8/beat-08.text: It was standing there the whole time.

logic-arguments-8/beat-09.text: This trap has a name: affirming the consequent. You spot the result, then claim the cause.

logic-arguments-8/beat-10.text: It breaks the instant anything else could have produced the same result.

logic-arguments-8/beat-11.text: Now flip it the other way. Tomorrow’s forecast promises no rain at all, so you plan on dry pavement and leave the umbrella by the door.

logic-arguments-8/beat-13.text: That’s trap two: denying the antecedent. Removing one cause does not remove the result, because the result had other doors it could come through.

logic-arguments-9/beat-00.text: Someone puts a claim up where everyone can read it. The quickest way to look like you’ve beaten it is never to go near it.

logic-arguments-9/beat-01.text: The first dodge aims at the arguer. It says “he failed maths at school, so ignore his budget”.

logic-arguments-9/beat-02.text: But a claim doesn’t get its truth from the mouth it came out of. The insult has answered nothing on the board.

logic-arguments-9/beat-03.text: The second dodge builds a flimsy copy first. Swap their real position for a weaker one nobody holds, knock that down, and take the bow.

logic-arguments-9/beat-04.text: You beat a scarecrow you put up yourself.

logic-arguments-9/beat-05.text: Now look at what’s actually happened. Two replies, a lot of noise, and the claim is still standing where it was, unread and unanswered.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-00.text: Why is there something rather than nothing? Metaphysics’ most famous question.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-02.text: Leibniz said nothing is ever just true for no reason. Point that rule at everything at once.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-03.text: Why this crowded universe rather than an empty one? He said nothing would have been simpler and easier.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-05.text: Try to reach nothing. Parmenides tried.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-06.text: Strip away objects, space, time and physics, and a dark void is still something. You can’t think about what is not without making it a thing.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-07.text: Science never even tries. It starts mid-game, explaining one state of the world by an earlier one.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-08.text: Science has to assume there are states and laws to begin with.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-00.text: A rose, a ruby, a flag. Nothing else about them matches, yet all three are red.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-02.text: Give whatever the three things share a card of its own, and call the card redness. Now the awkward question.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-04.text: Plato hung it up here, in a slot of its own. The perfect Red sits above every red thing and needs none of them to exist.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-05.text: Aristotle took it straight back down. He agreed redness is real, but it lives pinned in the things themselves.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-08.text: A third camp shrugs. They say nothing is shared, and “red” is a word you hang beside things that happen to look alike.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-09.text: The card touches none of them.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-00.text: Nearly every scrap of matter this man was born with has been replaced. The name under him has not moved once.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-02.text: Locke asks you to picture two of them. A prince, and a cobbler who walks in off the street having never once seen a palace.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-03.text: The plate above the prince holds all he can remember doing. Every room, every promise, the whole thread running back to his childhood.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-04.text: Overnight the whole thread leaves the prince and settles above the cobbler. Neither man has taken a step.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-09.text: Now watch the ground. Nobody moves, and yet the two names cross the floor and trade stands.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-10.text: The name goes where the memories went.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-00.text: Look inward right now. There’s a warmth, a sound, a thought about tomorrow, another thought about this sentence.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-01.text: The stream is easy to find.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-02.text: Descartes says one continuing thinker is having them. Doubt everything you like: somebody is doing the doubting.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-03.text: So: a box for the owner.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-04.text: Hume went looking and reported back that he could never catch it. Every time he tried, he found another perception instead.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-07.text: Buddhism reaches the same place by another road, and calls the fixed self anatta — an illusion. That invites the obvious overreach, so it goes on the table too.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-00.text: A scanner reads every atom of you, builds a perfect copy on Mars, and vaporises the original here. Step in?

metaphysics-being-13/beat-01.text: Say yes, and say it works. What travels is a chain, not a body — memories, intentions, one half-finished thought about lunch.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-02.text: Now the machine malfunctions and forgets to vaporise you. You walk out on Earth.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-03.text: Someone with your whole chain walks out on Mars. Neither is a copy of the other.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-05.text: Try to put the label on one of them. Nothing chooses, because the two branches are the same in every respect there is.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-06.text: Identity has to pick one thing, and continuity has just gone two ways.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-00.text: Four claims, all of them true. And five columns, one for each of the ways the world could consistently have gone.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-01.text: Now mark each claim in every world it survives. Two of the rows fill completely.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-02.text: Two of them come out patchy.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-03.text: A full row is a necessary truth. It could not have been otherwise, however you rearrange things.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-04.text: A patchy row just happens to be true here.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-06.text: The two full rows are not the same kind of thing. One of them you could have filled in without leaving your chair.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-00.text: One ball rolls up and strikes another, and the second rolls away. You’ve watched that ten thousand times.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-01.text: Hume asks what exactly you saw.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-02.text: You saw the first ball move. You saw it touch.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-03.text: You saw the second move. Three things, all of them plain, none of them the thing you’re after.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-04.text: Between the touch and the movement is where the causing is supposed to live. Slow the film to a single frame and look straight at it.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-06.text: Nothing but one thing after another, over and over, with no glue anywhere. Hume answers that the glue is real, and that the glue is in you.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-00.text: Two addicts, and everything about them is the same. Same craving, same dose, same chemistry doing the same thing.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-01.text: Now add what each of them thinks about his own wanting. One is behind it.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-02.text: The other is dragged along by a craving he hates.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-03.text: Frankfurt calls that second arrow a desire about a desire. You don’t only want things.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-04.text: You have views about what you want.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-06.text: So freedom is not about where the craving came from. It’s about whether the man stands behind the craving or is pulled by it.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-00.text: Mary knows every physical fact about colour. Wavelengths, cones, which neurons fire and in what order.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-02.text: But Mary has never seen colour. She’s lived her whole life in a room with nothing in it but black, white and grey.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-03.text: Today she opens the door and looks at a red rose. Something arrives that was not on the wall.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-05.text: How the brain sorts light is a hard question with an ordinary answer coming. Why any of it is felt at all is a different sort of question.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-00.text: Four things on the table. Three of them sit somewhere you can point to.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-01.text: Point at the apple and you’ve pointed at something. Same for the chair, same for the star.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-02.text: Now point at the number three. Not three apples.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-03.text: Not the mark chalked on a board. The number.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-04.text: And yet three is a prime number, and three was prime before anybody counted anything.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-06.text: Plato takes the obvious way out. The number exists, and the number does not live here.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-00.text: An apple, written out as everything true of it. Red, round, sweet, eighty grams, on this table.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-01.text: Take the colour away. It’s still an apple.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-02.text: Take the roundness, take the weight.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-03.text: That was the last card. Either something stands there or nothing does, and philosophers have never agreed which.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-04.text: Locke thought there had to be something underneath holding the properties together. He also admitted he could say nothing at all about it.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-07.text: Here’s the cost of saying there’s no peg. A second apple, matching the first in every property there is.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-00.text: There is a universe. There did not have to be one.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-01.text: Why something rather than nothing? The question has outlasted everyone who ever picked it up.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-02.text: Leibniz had a rule. Nothing is without a reason.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-03.text: Then he aimed the rule at existence itself. Why is there anything?

metaphysics-being-2/beat-04.text: Nothing would have been simpler. He was right about that much.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-05.text: Parmenides got there first and went the other way. Forget reasons for a moment.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-06.text: Ask whether nothing was ever an option at all. Here’s the fork he left: one way says “it is”, the other says “it is not”.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-08.text: So he tries it. He steps onto the second way — and there’s nothing there to step onto.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-09.text: What is not cannot be walked on, pointed at, or thought about. It doesn’t have the decency to be an option.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-00.text: One world, and the world is real. Nothing here denies the world exists.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-01.text: Now suppose a civilisation like ours learns to run a world on a computer.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-02.text: Not one world. Thousands, for research.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-03.text: Count the minds. Almost all the minds now sit inside a machine, and every mind believes otherwise.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-04.text: Here’s your token. Nobody aimed the token.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-05.text: It landed where most of the minds are.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-08.text: Two of those three say the grid never gets built. Extinction, or nobody bothering.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-00.text: A line, with you standing on the middle of it. The question is not whether time passes.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-02.text: Presentism says only this instant exists. Yesterday isn’t kept in some other place.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-03.text: Yesterday is nowhere at all. It’s over.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-04.text: The growing block keeps everything that’s happened and says the future isn’t written yet. The line gets longer.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-06.text: Eternalism keeps the lot. Every moment is out there, and now is just where you happen to be, like here is where you stand.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-08.text: Relativity leans this way. Two observers can disagree about what’s happening now, and that’s awkward if only now exists.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-00.text: A moment, drawn as a set of points. The track runs in, and there are two ways out of it.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-01.text: Rewind and run it again. Same world, same laws, same you.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-02.text: Three times, and it goes the same way each time.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-03.text: Hard determinism stops there. The other branch was never a live option, so nobody deserves blame for missing it.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-05.text: Compatibilism says the phrase was never about the replay. It asks whether you’d have gone the other way had you wanted to.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-07.text: Libertarians want a replay that could itself go the other way. But then nothing about you settles which branch the run takes.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-00.text: A ship kept in service for centuries. Whenever a plank rots, the dockyard takes it out and puts a new one in.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-01.text: Do that long enough and no original plank is left. Same name, same berth, same crew, no old wood.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-02.text: Then a collector admits he kept every plank they threw away, and has built a second ship out of them.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-04.text: Two tests that normally agree. Unbroken use points left.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-05.text: Original wood points right. Nothing on the stage decides between the two.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-07.text: Under it sits a harder question. When do parts make one thing at all?

metaphysics-being-23/beat-08.text: A pile of planks is not a ship.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-00.text: Here’s a heap of sand. Take one grain away.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-01.text: Still a heap, of course. One grain has never been the difference between a heap and no heap.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-02.text: So the rule is safe: removing a single grain never changes the verdict. Every step you’re about to see applies a rule you just agreed to.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-03.text: Keep applying it. Half the grains are gone and the lamp hasn’t flickered, because at no point did one grain do anything.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-05.text: One grain left, and the lamp still says it’s a heap. Every single step was fine and the destination is nonsense.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-06.text: So something you agreed to is wrong, and the culprit isn’t obvious.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-00.text: You almost missed the train. Ask what that almost is made of.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-01.text: Up to this morning your life runs along one road.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-02.text: Then the road forks. Philosophers call each way things could have gone a possible world.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-03.text: One is solid because you walked it. The rest are drawn thin.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-05.text: Necessary means true on every road. Possible means true on at least one.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-06.text: Then David Lewis asked the awkward question. How solid are the thin roads?

metaphysics-being-25/beat-08.text: Lewis meant it word for word. Real places, with a flesh and blood you on each of them.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-00.text: Two flammable gases combine, and the result puts out fires.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-01.text: Nobody had wetness. Somewhere between the parts and the whole it arrived.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-02.text: Here’s a smaller case. No single car is a traffic jam.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-03.text: Each driver only brakes a little behind the one ahead. The jam has a speed anyway.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-05.text: Weak emergence is surprising and still follows from the parts.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-07.text: Strong emergence is the bold claim. Some feature the parts could never have given.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-00.text: Gravity has never once failed. Never failing is different from having to hold.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-01.text: Here are two bags. Every marble in each of them is blue.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-02.text: In the second, a machine paints each one on the way in. In the first it just happened.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-03.text: David Hume saw only the pattern. For him, a law is the best short summary of what always happens.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-05.text: David Armstrong answered that a law is a real relation. Being heated makes a metal expand.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-07.text: A third answer keeps the must and moves it inside. Heavy things pull by their nature.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-00.text: Your mind came from somewhere. The usual answer is that dead matter got organised enough.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-01.text: Panpsychism answers differently. Mind was there all along, faint, at the bottom of nature.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-02.text: Not that rocks ponder or electrons dream. The simplest bits of matter carry the smallest spark.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-03.text: Physics says what matter does, never what matter is in itself. Panpsychism fills the gap with experience.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-05.text: Leibniz called the simplest things monads, each one shut, each one with a view of its own.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-07.text: An emergentist answers that mind appears only once matter is organised richly enough.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-00.text: Nobody is in the forest. The tree falls, and the old question arrives with it.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-01.text: Realism says the world has its nature without any mind. Mountains would stand there unwatched.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-02.text: Anti-realism says what counts as real leans on minds. In the boldest form, to exist is to be perceived.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-03.text: Berkeley set a trap. Try to picture an unseen tree, and the tree you picture is being seen.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-05.text: Doctor Johnson kicked a stone and said he had refuted Berkeley that way.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-07.text: Now suppose every conscious being blinks out at once. No mind is left anywhere.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-00.text: Plato said the apple in your hand is only half-real. It isn’t unreal, just stuck between being and not-being.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-01.text: Heraclitus said everything flows, like a river you can’t step in twice. That troubled Plato.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-02.text: You can’t know a thing that won’t hold still, so he split the world in two. Being holds still and can be known.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-04.text: Prisoners chained since birth take flickering shadows for the real world. One gets free, climbs into daylight, and sees the things themselves.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-05.text: Plato says the wall is where you live, and the Forms are what’s casting the shadows.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-07.text: Everything you can touch is a rough copy of something perfect. Two sticks are never exactly equal, but the idea of Equality always is.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-08.text: And you can know the thing that never changes, where the copy is only ever a good guess.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-00.text: The same questions for two and a half thousand years. Any of them answered yet?

metaphysics-being-30/beat-01.text: Science settles a question and moves on. Metaphysics is still arguing over claims raised in antiquity.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-02.text: The defence says progress here does not mean closed cases. It means sharper questions and fewer live options.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-03.text: Picture a cave mapped in the dark. Each expedition charts new passages and marks the dead ends.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-05.text: Travellers who come later start from your map rather than from nothing.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-07.text: Physics leans on time, cause, law and possibility. Working out what those are is not a physics experiment.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-00.text: One slab of cheese. Solid all the way through, and there’s nothing here to argue about yet.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-01.text: Now three holes. Nothing was added to the cheese.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-02.text: Something was taken away. And yet there are three more things here than before.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-03.text: You can count holes. You can measure one, call it deeper than the next, and be right.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-04.text: Everything you do with objects, you do with holes.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-06.text: So what did you count? There are only three things it could be.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-07.text: The cheese, the ring of cheese around each gap, or the empty gap itself.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-00.text: A universe containing two iron spheres and absolutely nothing else. No stars, no observer, no floor.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-02.text: They’re exactly alike. Same size, same metal, same age, same temperature, and neither one ever existed without the other.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-03.text: Even the relations match. Each is two miles from a sphere just like itself.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-04.text: Every description you write of one is a true description of the other.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-06.text: You can point at one sphere and call it sphere A. But you carried the label in from outside.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-07.text: Take the label away again and nothing in the universe has changed.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-00.text: Nine blocks, stacked. Nothing has happened yet, and nothing about this picture tells you which way time is running.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-01.text: Now the tower falls. You’ve watched a tower of blocks fall a thousand times and it needs no explaining.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-02.text: So run the film backwards. A heap of blocks gathers itself and stands up.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-03.text: You knew the film was wrong before this sentence was over.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-04.text: Here’s the strange part. Every single collision in that reversed film is legal.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-05.text: Take any two blocks knocking together and the reverse obeys the same laws.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-08.text: That’s the whole answer. Order is rare and mess is common.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-09.text: Anything moving at random wanders into the mess and never wanders back.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-00.text: A table. Solid, obvious, and not in any doubt.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-01.text: Ask the awkward question about it anyway.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-02.text: Not what made the table, and not who owns the table. What holds a table up?

metaphysics-being-34/beat-03.text: Not the legs. What makes the thing a table at all.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-04.text: The wood does. The table is real because the grain is arranged as it is, and philosophers call that grounding rather than causing.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-05.text: The wood is not earlier than the table. The wood is underneath it.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-06.text: So ask the wood the same question, and you get molecules. Ask those and you get atoms, which were named for being the thing you couldn’t cut.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-09.text: A level that rests on nothing is what fundamental means. Notice it’s not the same as smallest, and not the same as earliest.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-10.text: It’s about what holds what up.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-00.text: Here’s your life drawn as a line. You’re standing at the near end.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-01.text: Now walk back to 1925. Nothing in the idea of a visit is broken yet.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-02.text: You’re a tourist with an unusual travel agent.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-03.text: So you arrive, and you stop your grandparents meeting. Then you’re never born.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-04.text: Then nobody arrives. Then they meet, and you’re born, and you arrive.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-08.text: One answer keeps the line whole. You were always at 1925, and whatever you did there is already how it went.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-09.text: The gun jams. It always jammed.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-00.text: A hotel with endless rooms, and tonight every single one is taken. Then somebody walks in wanting a bed.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-02.text: That’s the whole proof. Room one goes to room two, room two to room three, and on forever.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-03.text: Nobody is homeless and room one is empty.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-04.text: It works because there is no last room to fall off the end of. Try it with a hundred rooms and guest one hundred is out on the street.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-07.text: Nothing here is an error. A part can be paired off one to one with the whole, and only an endless collection can do that.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-08.text: That’s why William Lane Craig argues no real thing could work like this. The maths is fine.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-09.text: Whether anything buildable behaves this way is a different question.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-00.text: One glass, one shelf, ninety years. The glass was never knocked, never dropped, and never broke.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-01.text: Ask whether it was fragile and everyone says yes without pausing. Now say what that yes was about.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-03.text: So try the obvious definition. Fragile means: if it is struck, it breaks.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-05.text: And a sorcerer is watching, ready to toughen it the instant anyone swings. The glass does not break.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-06.text: The glass is still as fragile as it ever was.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-09.text: That’s a strange thing for a fact to be. Something true of the glass is true because of an event that never happened and now never will.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-00.text: Three days on a bench, and one piece of clay for all of them.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-01.text: Monday the clay is a lump, and Tuesday the same clay is a vase. Wednesday the potter squashes the vase back into a lump.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-02.text: So the clay was here for three days, and the vase for one.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-04.text: And still the bars are different lengths, which is a fact about dates rather than about clay.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-05.text: Saul Kripke gave the tool. If two names pick out one thing, they could not have picked out two.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-00.text: The plant died because nobody watered it. That sentence is true, and nobody is a great many people.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-01.text: Here are four of them. Not one of them lifted a watering can all week.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-02.text: Ask what would have happened if each had watered it, and every answer is the same. The plant lives.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-04.text: The test that finds the gardener finds the king too, and a stranger three streets away.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-05.text: The test is old. David Hume wrote the line, and philosophers still reach for the same one.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-00.text: Say “nothing exists” and you’ve said too much. Parmenides found this snag twenty-five centuries ago, and it still bites.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-01.text: Try to deny non-being. Think of nothing, and it becomes the object of a thought, which needs something to be about.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-02.text: Each grab at nothing turns it into a thing.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-03.text: At Elea, Parmenides set out two ways. The way that is, and the way that is not.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-04.text: Parmenides throws out the second, because what is not can be neither known nor said. So only what is counts as real, and change is a trick of the senses.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-06.text: Follow it and the world freezes. To change, a thing would have to pass into or out of not-being, and that road is closed.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-07.text: So motion itself becomes an illusion. Aristotle later loosened the knot.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-00.text: Tomorrow either rains or does not rain. Nothing could sound safer.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-01.text: Logic has a rule: every statement is either true or false.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-02.text: Point that rule at tomorrow and one of the two is true already, today.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-03.text: Aristotle imagined two admirals arguing the night before a sea battle. One of them was right while they spoke.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-05.text: So Aristotle refused the rule here. Tomorrow's line is neither true nor false yet.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-07.text: There’s a cheaper door. Let the line be written, and deny that writing it forces anything.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-00.text: Move the whole universe three feet east. Everything in it, all at once.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-01.text: Newton thought space was a real container, there whether or not anything sat in it.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-02.text: Leibniz thought it was only the arrangement. No things, no space.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-03.text: So the two disagree about the shifted world, and about nothing you could measure.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-05.text: Look at the gaps. Every distance between every pair is unchanged.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-07.text: Newton had one reply left: spin a bucket of water and the surface climbs the wall.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-00.text: There is something rather than nothing. Leibniz asked why, and Heidegger called it the first question of all.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-01.text: Heidegger called the question fundamental to all of metaphysics. It isn’t about why one thing or another exists.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-02.text: It asks why there’s anything at all to ask about.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-03.text: Leibniz pressed it hardest. He said nothing is just true for no reason.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-04.text: Every fact has a reason somewhere. So what’s the reason for there being anything?

metaphysics-being-5/beat-06.text: And here comes the strange part. You are a thing that wonders what it is.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-07.text: Heidegger’s name for that is Dasein, and through you the universe turns round and asks about itself.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-00.text: Swap every plank of a ship, one at a time. When no original wood is left, is it the same ship or a new one?

metaphysics-being-6/beat-01.text: Athens kept Theseus’s ship for centuries, replacing each rotted plank with a fresh one. In the end, not one original board remained.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-02.text: Plutarch reports the quarrel it started.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-04.text: Philosophers split the word “same” in two. Qualitative sameness is sharing every feature, like two new coins.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-05.text: Numerical sameness is being the one thing you were yesterday. The ship keeps the second and loses the first.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-06.text: You’re the living proof. Almost every cell in your body has been replaced since you were the toddler in your old photos.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-07.text: Yet you call that child yourself.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-00.text: You have never once been anywhere but right now. Not yesterday or tomorrow, but always now.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-01.text: So where is yesterday keeping itself?

metaphysics-being-7/beat-02.text: Draw time as a road. Three slices hang along the road: yesterday, this second, tomorrow.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-03.text: It looks like a row of rooms you could stroll between.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-04.text: So stroll to yesterday and point at it. There’s nothing there but an empty frame.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-05.text: Yesterday is not filed away somewhere else. It’s nowhere at all.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-06.text: Tomorrow is worse. It hasn’t been built yet.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-07.text: Another empty frame, waiting on a moment that hasn’t happened.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-08.text: Only the middle frame is filled in — the one you’re standing in. That view has a name: presentism.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-09.text: Reality is one lit slice, and it keeps moving.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-10.text: Other thinkers say that picture is upside down. Think of a book.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-11.text: Page four hundred is no less printed than page one. You just happen to be reading here.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-13.text: All three fill in at once. That’s eternalism — the block universe.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-14.text: Every moment exists. The word “now” just means where you’re standing, as the word “here” means where you are.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-00.text: Think of the last thing you chose. Now picture it already on its way a thousand years before you were born.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-01.text: Every event gets pushed over by the one before it.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-02.text: The first domino went over long before you existed — your genes, your parents, the street you grew up on. That push has been travelling ever since.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-04.text: Hard determinists take the conclusion on the chin. Given everything that came before, they say, you could not have done otherwise.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-05.text: Not once. Not in your entire life.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-06.text: And there’s the domino with your name on it. It goes over right on schedule.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-07.text: The choice you’re proudest of was a sentence physics started centuries ago.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-08.text: One camp refuses. For them a real choice snaps the chain and starts a brand-new line that no earlier cause set going.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-10.text: A third camp shrugs at the whole fight. They think both sides picked the wrong test.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-11.text: Freedom was never about escaping causes. So what else could a free choice be?

metaphysics-being-8/beat-14.text: That camp has a name: compatibilism. David Hume, and later Harry Frankfurt, keep every cause and change the test.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-15.text: You act freely when the push comes from your own wants, not from a hand on your arm.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-00.text: Your brain weighs about three pounds and takes up space. Does the thought you’re having right now weigh anything at all?

metaphysics-being-9/beat-01.text: Descartes doubted everything he could, but he could not doubt he was thinking. So mind thinks and takes up no space, and body takes up space and does not think.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-04.text: Then decide to lift your arm. Something with no size and no position has to shove a physical limb.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-05.text: Descartes pointed to the pineal gland. His critics answered that a mind with no size has nothing to push with.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-06.text: So physicalists close the gap instead. Damage a brain and the memory, the mood, even the character change with it.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-07.text: That suggests the mind is not another substance. It is something the brain does, the way digestion is something the gut does.

political-political-1/beat-00.text: Why obey rules you never agreed to? Every state claims authority over you.

political-political-1/beat-01.text: Where does that power come from?

political-political-1/beat-02.text: Hobbes ran a thought experiment. Strip away every law, every court and every ruler.

political-political-1/beat-03.text: With nobody left to judge disputes, fear and rivalry collide. Hobbes says life turns “nasty, brutish, and short”.

political-political-1/beat-04.text: Even the weakest can kill the strongest, so each strikes first out of fear. Hobbes calls the result “a war of every man against every man”.

political-political-1/beat-05.text: The only way out is to authorise one sovereign to keep the peace.

political-political-1/beat-08.text: No one ever signed it on paper. The contract is a test of legitimacy, not a document.

political-political-1/beat-09.text: For Hobbes the covenant binds subjects, so there’s no right to revolt. Locke disagreed: when rulers betray people’s rights, the people may resist.

political-political-10/beat-00.text: Three people, three piles, and the tallest is three times the shortest. Is that unjust?

political-political-10/beat-01.text: Stare at it as long as you like: the picture on its own will not tell you.

political-political-10/beat-02.text: Locke starts before the piles exist. The world lies there unowned.

political-political-10/beat-03.text: You work a patch, the work is yours, so the patch is yours too. But he builds a brake into the rule: leave enough, and as good, for everyone else.

political-political-10/beat-04.text: So a pile is never only a pile. Under every one runs a record of how it got there.

political-political-10/beat-05.text: Taken from the common, traded, traded again, handed on as a gift.
