political-political-10/beat-06.text: Nozick reads only that strip. Was every step clean — a fair taking, then free trades, then a gift nobody was forced to give?

political-political-10/beat-07.text: Then the pile at the end is hers, however tall it stands.

political-political-10/beat-09.text: Rawls never looks at the strip at all. Lay a level across the tops and read one number — how high is the shortest pile?

political-political-10/beat-10.text: Inequality is fine by him, but only if it lifts whoever ends up at the bottom.

political-political-11/beat-00.text: Switch off every government tonight — no courts, no police, nobody in charge. By morning, what’s left of everybody?

political-political-11/beat-01.text: Answer that and you’ve already decided what state you can justify.

political-political-11/beat-02.text: Nobody thinks this happened in history. It’s an instrument: set it to a reading of human nature, and see what has to be built on top.

political-political-11/beat-03.text: Hobbes turns the dial to fearful. Everyone is roughly equal, so everyone can kill everyone, so everyone strikes first.

political-political-11/beat-04.text: Only a power standing above the quarrel can stop it, and that power must be too tall to reach over.

political-political-11/beat-06.text: Locke turns it to rational. People already owe each other things out here, and all that’s missing is a neutral judge.

political-political-11/beat-07.text: So he builds small, and the people stay outside it holding the rights they walked in with.

political-political-11/beat-08.text: Rousseau turns it to innocent. People were fine until property and rank taught them to compare themselves.

political-political-11/beat-09.text: Rousseau's answer has no one at the top at all. Everybody is bound to the common good.

political-political-11/beat-10.text: That’s how he means to hand freedom back.

political-political-12/beat-00.text: Rousseau wrote that a people can be forced to be free. The phrase sounds like nonsense.

political-political-12/beat-01.text: Isaiah Berlin spent an essay explaining why the phrase makes sense, and why that’s worse.

political-political-12/beat-02.text: Freedom question one: how many doors are open to you, with nobody standing in them? That is negative liberty, and it is entirely about what other people are doing.

political-political-12/beat-03.text: Open the door and the first lamp lights. Nothing is blocking you.

political-political-12/beat-04.text: The definition says nothing about whether you can walk through the door.

political-political-12/beat-06.text: Here’s Berlin’s worry. A regime announces that your real self wants the regime’s plan.

political-political-12/beat-07.text: The regime lights the second lamp on your behalf, shuts the door, and calls the result freedom.

political-political-13/beat-00.text: Mill gives only one reason for using power over a person against their will. To stop them harming somebody else.

political-political-13/beat-01.text: Not for their own good, and not because you dislike the choice.

political-political-13/beat-02.text: A speaker says something most of the town finds repellent. Nobody is assaulted, nothing is stolen, no threat is made.

political-political-13/beat-03.text: The town wants them stopped, and here’s the argument.

political-political-13/beat-04.text: Three steps. Read them in order and the argument feels like a proof.

political-political-13/beat-05.text: Each one seems to follow from the one before. And the conclusion is what the town wanted.

political-political-13/beat-07.text: Mill grants the first: they’re certainly offended. He grants the third, since it’s his own principle.

political-political-13/beat-08.text: So the whole weight of the town's case is resting on the middle one.

political-political-14/beat-00.text: Start from any distribution you’re willing to call just, dead equal if you like. Nozick doesn’t mind, and that’s the point of letting you choose.

political-political-14/beat-01.text: Now a basketball star offers to play, and asks a dollar from anyone who wants to watch. A million people happily pay.

political-political-14/beat-03.text: And the pattern is gone. He’s vastly rich, everyone else is a dollar poorer, and nobody was wronged at any step of it.

political-political-14/beat-05.text: So if you want the top row back, you have to reach into this picture and stop something. Nozick's question is only which row you were planning to reach into.

political-political-15/beat-00.text: Breaking a law can be the most law-respecting thing a person does. But the conditions are strict, and most lawbreaking fails them.

political-political-15/beat-01.text: Name the injustice, and try the lawful routes first. Petitions, courts, elections.

political-political-15/beat-02.text: Skipping this is where most claims to civil disobedience fall over.

political-political-15/beat-03.text: Then break the law, in daylight, without violence. And then the one that does the real work: stay, and take the punishment the law hands you.

political-political-15/beat-05.text: Now a protest names the injustice, tries the courts and breaks the law, then goes home by a back route. Lay it against the stair and count.

political-political-16/beat-00.text: You fit the same bolt all day. Four things are wired to that work.

political-political-16/beat-01.text: The thing you make, the doing of it, what you could be, everyone beside you.

political-political-16/beat-02.text: The car goes to the company and you couldn’t afford one. The line sets the pace and you cannot stop it.

political-political-16/beat-04.text: The other two follow. Nothing you could have made is being made, and the people beside you are competitors for the same shift.

political-political-16/beat-06.text: Marx says none of that is about the wage. It follows from who owns the machines and who decides what happens on the floor.

political-political-17/beat-00.text: A village digs a well together and keeps a rota. Everyone hauls, everyone drinks, and nobody signed anything.

political-political-17/beat-01.text: A newcomer drinks from it daily. His row on the rota is empty, and when his turn comes he points at that.

political-political-17/beat-02.text: The newcomer is right about the signature. Almost nobody has ever agreed to the state they live under either, which is the awkward part.

political-political-17/beat-04.text: So fair play stops asking about signatures. If you take what a shared effort produces, you owe your share of producing it.

political-political-18/beat-00.text: Two people, one bicycle each, and the bicycles are identical. So far this is as equal as anything gets.

political-political-18/beat-01.text: Now let them go. One crosses the city.

political-political-18/beat-02.text: The other can’t use their legs and gets almost nowhere at all.

political-political-18/beat-03.text: Nothing unfair happened at the start: the resource was equal. It turned into wildly different amounts of getting about.

political-political-18/beat-05.text: So Sen moves the question. He says to stop measuring what people hold and measure what their lives actually let them do.

political-political-19/beat-00.text: A child is drowning in a pond at your feet. You wade in and ruin a good pair of shoes.

political-political-19/beat-01.text: The top panel is what it costs you. Across the whole distance, it’s the price of the shoes.

political-political-19/beat-02.text: The bottom panel is how strongly you feel you must act. Watch what happens to it.

political-political-19/beat-03.text: Same child, same money, same certainty that the money helps. The only thing that changed is where you’re standing.

political-political-19/beat-06.text: The trouble is where that principle stops. There’s always one more preventable death for the price of one more thing you own.

political-political-2/beat-00.text: Force can make you obey. Can it make you agree?

political-political-2/beat-01.text: Power bends bodies, but authority wins minds. They are not the same thing.

political-political-2/beat-02.text: Weber split two ideas people usually blur together. Power gets its way despite resistance, by threat or force, and a mugger has it.

political-political-2/beat-03.text: Authority is being obeyed because people think you’re entitled to be.

political-political-2/beat-04.text: Augustine sharpened the point. A captured pirate told Alexander, “With one ship I’m a robber, and you with a fleet are an emperor.”

political-political-2/beat-05.text: Both take by threat — only legitimacy tells them apart.

political-political-2/beat-07.text: Weber sorted legitimacy into three sources. Tradition leans on custom and bloodline.

political-political-2/beat-08.text: Charisma runs on devotion to one person. The third kind rests on rules and offices, where power sits in the job rather than the holder.

political-political-20/beat-00.text: Two neighbours. Everything either of them believes about how to live is in one of those stacks.

political-political-20/beat-01.text: They overlap almost nowhere, and neither is going to talk the other round. This is not a failure.

political-political-20/beat-02.text: Rawls thought it was the normal result of free thinking.

political-political-20/beat-03.text: They still have to share a street, and a law about the street will land on both of them.

political-political-20/beat-04.text: So the shelf. A reason for the law has to be one the other person could weigh without first joining you.

political-political-20/beat-07.text: Look at the size of the shelf. Almost everything either side cares about stayed in its own stack.

political-political-21/beat-00.text: You never signed anything. No state has ever had your signature on a page.

political-political-21/beat-01.text: The usual answer is that you agreed by staying. Carry on living here and you’ve accepted the terms.

political-political-21/beat-02.text: So try leaving. Hop to the next square and somebody already governs it.

political-political-21/beat-04.text: There’s only one square nobody has claimed, and you can’t live on it.

political-political-21/beat-07.text: Philosophical anarchism stops right there. The view does not call for a riot.

political-political-21/beat-08.text: The view says the state never earned the authority it claims.

political-political-22/beat-00.text: A servant with a kind employer. He has never once ordered her about.

political-political-22/beat-01.text: The servant's day is her own.

political-political-22/beat-02.text: The switch is on his wall, and only he can reach the switch. His reach does not go away while he leaves the lever alone.

political-political-22/beat-03.text: If he ever felt like it, here’s what happens, and there’s nothing whatever she could do.

political-political-22/beat-05.text: One question asks whether anyone is interfering now. The other asks whether anyone could, whenever they liked.

political-political-22/beat-07.text: So the cure is not better manners from the powerful. It is courts, rights and rules that take the switch off the wall.

political-political-23/beat-00.text: Three things you are. Two of them you signed up for.

political-political-23/beat-01.text: One was true before you could speak.

political-political-23/beat-02.text: Now set them aside. To pick fair rules, Rawls asks you to forget your class, your faith and your history.

political-political-23/beat-03.text: The liberal picture says a chooser is still in there. You exist first, then pick what to care about.

political-political-23/beat-05.text: The other side says that once the ties come off, nothing neutral is left underneath to do the choosing.

political-political-23/beat-07.text: Morality only makes sense inside a tradition. Asked to choose values from nowhere, a person has no compass at all.

political-political-24/beat-00.text: A minority language. It’s printed on the court papers and taught in the schools, and at home it’s spoken.

political-political-24/beat-01.text: Recognition is not a courtesy added on top. You become who you are through how the people around you see you.

political-political-24/beat-02.text: Take the language out of the public places and leave the goodwill. Five generations later, this is what’s left.

political-political-24/beat-04.text: Being mirrored back as lesser, or not at all, can trap people inside a picture of themselves they never made.

political-political-24/beat-06.text: Two demands pull apart here. Treat everybody identically, or recognise what makes each way of life its own thing.

political-political-25/beat-00.text: Who does the dishes turns out to be a question about justice.

political-political-25/beat-01.text: Political philosophy used to draw a line at the front door.

political-political-25/beat-02.text: Law, work and the vote were public, and open to argument.

political-political-25/beat-03.text: What happened at home was private, and treated as nature rather than power.

political-political-25/beat-05.text: Feminist thinkers turned the line around. What’s private is held there by public rules.

political-political-25/beat-06.text: A mother quits work when parental leave favours her and childcare costs more than she earns.

political-political-25/beat-08.text: Susan Okin put the point to Rawls. Behind the veil you can’t know your gender either.

political-political-26/beat-00.text: A vote can count millions of opinions and weigh not one of them.

political-political-26/beat-01.text: One picture of democracy is a machine that adds up whatever people already want.

political-political-26/beat-02.text: Jürgen Habermas put the legitimacy earlier, in the reasons citizens give each other.

political-political-26/beat-03.text: A decision binds you justly when it could be defended to everyone it lands on.

political-political-26/beat-05.text: A citizens’ assembly hears experts for weeks and questions itself. Many arrive fixed and leave moved.

political-political-26/beat-07.text: Critics answer that talk favours the articulate, where one vote each treats people as equals.

political-political-27/beat-00.text: Pacifists say war is never right. Realists say the rules stop at the border.

political-political-27/beat-01.text: Just war theory sits between them and hangs two gates across one road.

political-political-27/beat-02.text: The first gate asks whether going to war is justified. A just cause, a last resort, and no better option.

political-political-27/beat-03.text: The second gate asks how the fighting is done. Spare civilians, and use no more force than the job needs.

political-political-27/beat-05.text: A country is invaded and fights back, then firebombs an enemy city to end the war sooner.

political-political-27/beat-07.text: Augustine argued a war could be just. Aquinas set out the tests: right authority, right cause, right intention.

political-political-28/beat-00.text: The state takes years of a life. Everyone else is forbidden to do anything like it.

political-political-28/beat-01.text: Punishment does on purpose what the law forbids everyone else. So the state needs a reason nobody else can use.

political-political-28/beat-02.text: One answer looks back. He did it, so the sentence is what he’s earned.

political-political-28/beat-03.text: The other looks forward. Punishment is there to deter, to protect, and to send somebody back changed.

political-political-28/beat-04.text: A town is rioting. Framing one innocent man would calm the mob and save many lives.

political-political-28/beat-07.text: Foucault refused the whole frame. He asked not whether prison is justified, but what a prison does.

political-political-29/beat-00.text: The luckiest thing that ever happened to you may be where you were born.

political-political-29/beat-01.text: Two babies are born the same day. One inside a wealthy democracy, one just across the line.

political-political-29/beat-02.text: Neither did anything to deserve a side. Carens calls citizenship the modern form of feudal privilege.

political-political-29/beat-03.text: An inherited status that shapes a life, handed out by birth. Liberal states reject that kind of rank at home.

political-political-29/beat-05.text: Walzer answers back. A community is partly defined by the power to admit or refuse.

political-political-29/beat-07.text: Without control over membership, a self-governing people stops meaning anything at all.

political-political-3/beat-00.text: A gun makes you obey. What makes you owe obedience?

political-political-3/beat-01.text: Power compels. Legitimacy is the other thing, and the gap between them is the whole subject.

political-political-3/beat-02.text: Imagine no state at all — people free and unruled. Hobbes argued that with no common judge, this “state of nature” slides into war.

political-political-3/beat-03.text: So people covenant to set up a ruler who keeps the peace.

political-political-3/beat-04.text: Locke said people set up a government to guard their rights, and it holds power only in trust. Break the trust and the government forfeits its right to rule.

political-political-3/beat-05.text: The American founders leaned on Locke in 1776.

political-political-3/beat-07.text: Rousseau pushed further. Legitimacy flows from what he called the “general will” — what serves everyone, not the sum of private wants.

political-political-3/beat-08.text: Real freedom is living under rules you give yourself.

political-political-30/beat-00.text: Picture the perfect society, or abolish the nearest injustice. Every theory meets this question in the end.

political-political-30/beat-01.text: Ideal theory asks what perfect justice would look like. Rawls began there and built the model first.

political-political-30/beat-02.text: Non-ideal theory starts from the world as it is. Amartya Sen asks what to do about the wrongs already standing.

political-political-30/beat-03.text: To judge one painting better than another, you do not first need the greatest painting there is.

political-political-30/beat-05.text: People suffering now cannot wait for a blueprint that may never arrive.

political-political-30/beat-07.text: Rawls answers that without a target, reform drifts. A compass is not a fantasy.

political-political-31/beat-00.text: A field nobody owns and everybody may use. Deep grass, one animal on it, and four herders who all have the same right to be here.

political-political-31/beat-01.text: You put on one more. The whole of what it eats is yours, but the wear on the grass falls on all four of you.

political-political-31/beat-02.text: It is a good trade, and you would be daft not to make it.

political-political-31/beat-03.text: So does everyone else, for the same reason. Now the field is bare, every herder is worse off than before, and nobody has done a single unreasonable thing.

political-political-31/beat-05.text: Here’s the sum each of them did. One whole unit of gain, all of it kept.

political-political-31/beat-06.text: One whole unit of damage, cut into four. Nothing else was required.

political-political-32/beat-00.text: The count is coming in. Two piles of marks, each one somebody who got up and went out on a wet Thursday.

political-political-32/beat-01.text: And it’s settled. The result would have been the same if any one of these marks had never been made.

political-political-32/beat-02.text: Including yours. The odds of a single vote deciding a national election are worse than most lotteries.

political-political-32/beat-03.text: You knew that on the way to the hall.

political-political-32/beat-05.text: But deciding the winner is not the only thing a mark can do. Look at the gap between the two piles, where the top row has nothing under it.

political-political-33/beat-00.text: A society decides which ideas to let in. The doors are that decision, and right now the doors stand open to most things.

political-political-33/beat-01.text: Open the doors all the way and everything is admitted. Every argument gets a hearing, which is what a free society is for.

political-political-33/beat-02.text: Then something walks through intending to shut the doors behind it. Karl Popper noticed the trap in 1945.

political-political-33/beat-03.text: Unlimited tolerance can be used to end tolerance.

political-political-33/beat-04.text: So shut the doors. Now look at what you’ve built.

political-political-33/beat-05.text: A society deciding in advance which arguments may be heard has become what you set out to prevent.

political-political-33/beat-08.text: Notice what the test turns on. Not what a movement believes, which anyone can label, but whether it will meet you in an argument at all.

political-political-34/beat-00.text: Five rings, from you in the middle out to everybody. Every political question has to be answered in one of them.

political-political-34/beat-01.text: Some are easy. What you eat for breakfast affects you, so the ring that decides it is the small one, and nobody argues.

political-political-34/beat-02.text: Now a village decides to put its waste in the river. That’s a very local decision about something that isn’t local at all.

political-political-34/beat-03.text: And it goes wrong the other way too. A distant office setting one school’s timetable has all the authority and none of the knowledge.

political-political-34/beat-06.text: That is subsidiarity, and it has two halves. As small as possible is only the first one.

political-political-34/beat-07.text: The second says the room can be no smaller than the problem.

political-political-35/beat-00.text: A room where a decision gets made. Three people are in it.

political-political-35/beat-01.text: Nine of the chairs belong to people who are not born yet.

political-political-35/beat-03.text: So far the choice is merely hard. Now comes the strange part.

political-political-35/beat-04.text: Pick the reckless policy and the world runs another way. Other jobs, other journeys, other couples meeting.

political-political-35/beat-06.text: Watch who’s in the room now. Not the same three.

political-political-35/beat-07.text: Under the careful policy these people were never born at all.

political-political-35/beat-10.text: One reply drops the search for a victim. Some choices make the world go worse, and that’s a reason not to make them.

political-political-36/beat-00.text: A street at night. Behind every lit window a person is doing something plain and legal.

political-political-36/beat-02.text: So the slogan “nothing to hide, nothing to fear” answers a question nobody asked. The cost lands on people doing nothing wrong.

political-political-36/beat-03.text: Bentham drew a prison where one guard could see every cell and no prisoner could tell if he was looking. Look at the box.

political-political-36/beat-07.text: Nothing here shows up in a statistic. No case was brought.

political-political-36/beat-08.text: What shrank was the range of things people were willing to try.

political-political-36/beat-09.text: So privacy isn’t mainly about secrets. Privacy is how much room a person has when nobody is judging them.

political-political-37/beat-00.text: Two citizens on election day. Two ballots, drawn the same size, because they are the same size.

political-political-37/beat-01.text: Now look above the ballots. One of them can be heard across the country.

political-political-37/beat-02.text: The other can be heard across a room.

political-political-37/beat-04.text: Rawls put it as a distinction. Having a liberty is one thing.

political-political-37/beat-05.text: Being able to use the right is another. Only one of the two is equal here.

political-political-37/beat-08.text: So the argument never settles. One side defends the right to be heard.

political-political-37/beat-09.text: So does the other. The two sides disagree about whose right it is.

political-political-37/beat-10.text: Every democracy draws the line somewhere, usually without announcing it. Where the line lands tells you what a country thinks a vote is for.

political-political-38/beat-00.text: You elect somebody. Months later a vote comes up that nobody mentioned in the campaign.

political-political-38/beat-01.text: There’s a cord between the two of you, and the only question is how much slack it has.

political-political-38/beat-02.text: Here are three things he might owe you.

political-political-38/beat-04.text: In 1774 Edmund Burke faced the voters of Bristol on election day. He told them that instructions were not part of the bargain.

political-political-38/beat-05.text: The voters returned Burke once, then threw him out. That’s the other half of the argument.

political-political-39/beat-00.text: Sixty said yes and forty said no. You were one of the forty.

political-political-39/beat-01.text: And now it is the law, including for you. Something has to join a count to an obligation, and being outnumbered will not.

political-political-39/beat-02.text: Four things get offered. Three of them are arguments.

political-political-39/beat-04.text: Power makes you comply. Authority gives you a reason you’d still hold with nobody watching.

political-political-39/beat-05.text: John Locke put the case for the count itself. A body that needs unanimous consent to move never moves.

political-political-4/beat-00.text: Free because no one stops you, or free because you can? Two ideas of freedom — and two very different politics.

political-political-4/beat-01.text: Berlin called this negative liberty: the area where others leave you alone. The walls pull back.

political-political-4/beat-02.text: Mill drew the line — power may be used against you only to prevent harm to others.

political-political-4/beat-03.text: Eat badly, take wild risks, preach unpopular views? Mill says that’s your business.

political-political-4/beat-04.text: But poison a well, defraud a buyer, throw a punch? Now you harm others, and only then may power step in.

political-political-4/beat-06.text: Berlin named a rival ideal: positive liberty — being your own master. You might face no interference yet still be too poor, sick, or untaught to act.

political-political-4/beat-07.text: Should the state empower people, not merely leave them alone?

political-political-40/beat-00.text: Two willing people agree a fair price for a vote. Nobody is poor, and nobody is fooled.

political-political-40/beat-01.text: The usual complaint about markets is unfairness. That one doesn’t fit here.

political-political-40/beat-02.text: So there’s a second complaint underneath the first, and it’s about the goods themselves.

political-political-40/beat-03.text: Some things are changed by being priced. What the buyer gets is not what they wanted.

political-political-40/beat-05.text: Firms will hold your place in a queue for a hearing. Everybody involved agrees.

political-political-40/beat-07.text: A queue was a place where turning up early was the only thing that counted.

political-political-41/beat-00.text: A constitution is a stack of rules written before anything happened.

political-political-41/beat-01.text: Then a fire, a plague or an invasion arrives, and no page covers it.

political-political-41/beat-02.text: John Locke gave the executive room to act anyway. He called it prerogative.

political-political-41/beat-03.text: The power has an owner and a purpose. One slot is left conspicuously empty.

political-political-41/beat-05.text: Legislatures are slow, and an emergency doesn’t wait for a session.

political-political-41/beat-07.text: Locke tied the power to the need, so that the need could be argued about afterwards.

political-political-5/beat-00.text: What makes a whole society just? Plato asked it some twenty-four centuries ago, and people are still arguing.

political-political-5/beat-01.text: Plato asks what a just city would look like. His answer: everyone does the work they’re suited to, and nobody meddles.

political-political-5/beat-02.text: Ruling goes to philosopher-kings, the only people he thinks know the good.

political-political-5/beat-04.text: Rawls asks it another way. What rules would you pick if you didn’t know who you were going to be?

political-political-5/beat-05.text: Hide your class, your talents and your luck behind a veil, and watch how fair your choices get.

political-political-5/beat-07.text: Watch the big questions link up. Hobbes asks why people build societies.

political-political-5/beat-08.text: Locke and Rousseau ask what makes them legitimate. Mill asks how far they may bind you.

political-political-5/beat-09.text: Plato and Rawls ask what justice demands.

political-political-6/beat-00.text: Would you accept this society if you turned out to be the poorest in it? Rawls turned that question into a test for justice itself.

political-political-6/beat-01.text: Back behind the veil of ignorance, you choose the rules not knowing who you’ll be. Rawls says two principles fall out of that fair start, in strict order.

political-political-6/beat-02.text: First: each person gets the same basic liberties, and these come first. Second: inequalities are allowed only if they help the least advantaged and attach to jobs open to all.

political-political-6/beat-04.text: Is a surgeon earning far more than a clerk unjust? Not necessarily.

political-political-6/beat-05.text: The gap is just when higher pay draws talent that lifts even the worst-off above the equality line. The test is the bottom, not the top.

political-political-7/beat-00.text: You’re allowed to say what you think. So who handed you that?

political-political-7/beat-01.text: A government? A piece of paper?

political-political-7/beat-02.text: Or was it yours before anyone voted on anything?

political-political-7/beat-03.text: John Locke pointed at the ground. Some things are yours the moment you exist — your life, your freedom, your stuff.

political-political-7/beat-04.text: Nobody grants your rights. A government exists to guard them, not to hand them out.

political-political-7/beat-05.text: Others pointed up here instead. A right is something people wrote down, signed, and agreed to enforce.

political-political-7/beat-06.text: No signature, no right — just a wish said loudly.

political-political-7/beat-08.text: Here’s how to tell the two apart. Tomorrow a government passes a law: from now on, you may not say what you think.

political-political-7/beat-09.text: The law is real, and it’s enforced.

political-political-7/beat-11.text: Watch what the law can reach. It tears the paper in half, and the stone does not move.

political-political-7/beat-12.text: That’s the claim: rights you have just for being human. A government can break one.

political-political-7/beat-15.text: And the claim has teeth. Thinkers announced the rights of man, then quietly stopped at men.

political-political-7/beat-16.text: Mary Wollstonecraft pressed the logic: if rights come from being a reasoning human, women are that too.

political-political-8/beat-01.text: A match on the far side that all three want to watch. Everybody agrees they should get to.

political-political-8/beat-02.text: Now watch how fast agreeing falls apart.

political-political-8/beat-03.text: Nobody here cheated anybody. They were born different heights.

political-political-8/beat-04.text: The tall one sees the whole pitch. The short one sees a plank of wood.

political-political-8/beat-05.text: Luckily somebody left three crates by the gate. Three crates, three people.

political-political-8/beat-06.text: You can’t get fairer than one each. Can you?

political-political-8/beat-07.text: One crate each. Same size, same share, nobody favoured, nobody skipped.

political-political-8/beat-08.text: And the shortest one is still looking at wood.

political-political-8/beat-10.text: Nothing was added and nothing was thrown away. The same three crates, moved to where they actually do something.

political-political-8/beat-11.text: Look at the eye line now — dead level.

political-political-8/beat-13.text: So equality is a blank waiting to be filled in. Equal resources?

political-political-8/beat-15.text: Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum answer differently. Make capabilities equal: what a person can really do and be.

political-political-9/beat-00.text: Rule by the people. Four of them here, and one over there who wants something the four do not.

political-political-9/beat-01.text: So they vote, and the count is honest, and the count is four to one. Plato distrusted this: steering a ship takes a trained pilot, not a show of hands.

political-political-9/beat-02.text: Let the crew vote and they follow whoever flatters them best.

political-political-9/beat-03.text: Nothing has gone wrong with the procedure. Everyone got a vote, the larger number won, and now the larger number is walking toward the smaller one.

political-political-9/beat-04.text: This is democracy working, not democracy failing.

political-political-9/beat-06.text: Mill and Tocqueville both named the danger, and both drew a line no vote can cross. That’s why a court can strike down a law the majority voted for.
